client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. It takes something to walk through that door, especially right after detox. I just want you to know there's no agenda here, no checklist we have to get through. So... I guess I'm curious, in your own words — what's on your mind coming into this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm here because my wife said if I didn't come she was done. So. Here I am. I'm not gonna pretend otherwise.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She matters enough to you that you showed up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. But look, I want to be clear — I don't think I have some kind of, like, alcoholic problem the way people picture it. Where I came from, you drink. After a deployment, after a loss, after whatever — you drink. That's just... that's the culture. That's how it works. I did what everybody did.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It was woven into everything — the camaraderie, the way you dealt with what happened over there. It wasn't separate from being a soldier, it was part of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly that. You'd come back from... from whatever you saw that day, and somebody hands you a beer, and for a couple hours you're not thinking about it. You're just — you're with your guys. You're laughing. You're not back there. And nobody told us that was wrong. Nobody pulled us aside and said hey, you might want to watch that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gave you relief when nothing else did. And no one ever taught you there might be a cost to that down the road.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And then you get home and... it's different. It doesn't — the stuff you're trying not to think about, it doesn't go away just because you're stateside. So you keep doing what worked. Except I guess, um... it stopped working at some point and I didn't really notice. Or I noticed and just didn't want to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to say. I'm wondering... you mentioned your wife. What does it look like if things don't change? What's actually at stake for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I lose everything. I mean... she's not bluffing. I know her. And my kids — I got two kids, six and nine — they've been watching me, you know? My son, he started getting real quiet around me and I... I don't know when that happened. That's the part that keeps me up at night more than anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your son pulling away from you — that landed somewhere deep. It sounds like being the kind of father they deserve, that's something you care about fiercely.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't join the Army to come home and be... this. I wanted to give them something. Security, you know, a dad who showed up. My own father wasn't around much and I swore I wouldn't be that. And then I look up and I'm... I'm not sure what I've been giving them. That's hard to sit with.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You had a picture in your head of who you were going to be for them. What would it mean to get closer to that — even just a little bit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think my kid would look at me different. That's what I want, more than anything. I want him to not be scared of me or whatever he's feeling. I want to go to one of his baseball games sober and actually be there. Not just standing in the bleachers somewhere else in my head.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You went through detox — that's not easy, physically or any other way. And you're still here, in this chair, talking about your son's baseball game. That took real strength, even if it doesn't feel like it right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Detox was... yeah. That was rough. I've been through some things but that was its own kind of hard. I'm not gonna lie, there were moments I wanted to walk out. But I kept thinking, if I leave I don't have an answer for her, for them. And I didn't want to not have an answer anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You stayed because you wanted something different, not just because someone told you to. That's yours. So when you imagine things actually being different — what does that look like, even if it feels far away?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to wake up and not immediately think about when the next drink is. That sounds small but... that's it. Just — mornings where I'm just a guy making coffee. And maybe my wife stops looking at me like she's waiting for the other shoe to drop. I think we could get back to something if I could just... stay steady.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think you've said some important things today. You came in feeling like you had to be here, and somewhere in this hour you found your own reasons — your son watching you from the bleachers, mornings that feel like mornings, getting back to something with your wife. You're not here because drinking was never a solution — it was, for a time, in a situation where very few solutions existed. And now you're looking at what that cost, and deciding if there's a different way to carry what you carry. That takes real courage to look at straight. How are you feeling sitting with all of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I feel like... I don't know, like maybe this isn't totally pointless. Which is more than I thought I'd feel walking in here. So that's something, I guess.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back. That took something, and I don't want to gloss over that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... Linda said she'd leave if I didn't. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She matters to you. Even if the push came from her, you still walked through that door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know what she sees in me at this point, honestly. Three years. Three years sober and then... I just threw it all away. Over what? Because I lost a job? My dad lost jobs. He didn't... he didn't fall apart like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're being really hard on yourself right now. Comparing yourself to your father, measuring your worth against those three years like they don't count anymore. What was it like when you got that call — when you found out you'd lost the job?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was like... the floor just disappeared. I'd been there nineteen years. Nineteen. And they sent me a Teams message. Not even a phone call. A message. And I just sat there in the driveway for like an hour and then I went and bought a bottle and that was that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nineteen years and a Teams message.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — I mean when you say it like that it sounds almost... I don't know. I keep telling myself I should've been stronger. But hearing it out loud like that. That was brutal. That was genuinely brutal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you're starting to make a little room for some compassion for yourself. What do you think kept you sober for those three years? What was working?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: AA, for one. I had a sponsor, Dennis. Good man. And... honestly? Work. Work was my structure. I had somewhere to be every morning at seven. I had a reason to not drink the night before. Take that away and I just — I didn't have anything to hold onto.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So structure and connection — Dennis, the meetings, even your routine at work — those were the things that held you up. And when the job vanished, it took a lot of that scaffolding with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't called Dennis since it happened. I'm... I'm ashamed to. He was so proud of me. Everyone was. And now I've got to go back and say what, 'hey, day one again, sorry'? I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The shame is keeping you away from the very people who've supported you through hard things before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... God. Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's exactly what's happening, isn't it. That's the trap. I've heard that before, actually. In meetings. Someone said shame is the thing that keeps you drinking because it keeps you alone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You remembered that. Even now, you're drawing on what you learned. That knowledge didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I do still know how this works. I'm not starting from zero on everything, am I. It just feels that way. It really, really feels that way some mornings.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feeling is real, and I'm not going to dismiss it. But you also just named your sponsor, you named what worked, you recognized the shame trap the moment I reflected it back. What would it mean to reach out to Dennis — even just a text?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He'd probably just say... come to a meeting. That's what he always said. Keep it simple, Frank. Just come to a meeting. Maybe — I don't know. Maybe I could do that. Linda would probably cry. In a good way, I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today for Linda, maybe. But just now, thinking about calling Dennis, picturing her face — that sounds like it might also be for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Maybe it is. I used to be someone who showed up for himself. I want to be that guy again. I really do.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Marcus. You can sit wherever — I know that couch looks like it belongs in a dentist's waiting room, sorry about that. So... your parents dragged you here, huh?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I didn't really have a choice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right. Not exactly how most people choose to spend a Thursday afternoon. And look — I'm not gonna pretend you wanted to be here, 'cause that'd be insulting. What I am curious about is... what's going through your head right now, sitting in this room?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Nothing. That this is stupid, I guess. Like, I'm not some... addict or whatever. My parents totally overreacted, found a few bottles and now suddenly I'm in therapy. It's fine. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A few bottles, parents freak out, suddenly you're the problem. That feels really unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is unfair. Like... yeah. I mean, my dad drinks at dinner every single night and nobody's sending him to therapy, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real observation — you're noticing something that genuinely doesn't add up to you. I want to hear more about that. But I also heard you just went through a detox program, which is... that's not nothing. That's actually pretty hard, and you did it. What was that like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I mean. It sucked. It really sucked. I didn't think it would be like that, I thought it was just gonna be like, sitting around talking. But my hands were shaking and I couldn't sleep and... whatever. I got through it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Shaking hands, no sleep, sixteen years old. You got through something that grown adults struggle with. I want you to hold onto that for a second — that took real grit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I guess. It doesn't feel like grit. It just feels like I messed everything up and now I have to fix it. Or like, they want me to fix it. I don't even know what I want.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't know what you want. That's actually a really honest thing to say — most kids who come in here act like they've got it all figured out, and it's usually the ones who say 'I don't know' who are actually thinking. So... when did drinking start feeling like something you needed, not just something you did at a party or whatever?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, like... sophomore year got really bad. With school, and my parents were fighting a lot, and I just... it was like the only time my brain would shut up, you know? Like everything would just go quiet for a while. And then I needed more of it to get that feeling and then... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it started as a way to get some peace. Some quiet from everything that was loud — school, your parents, your own head. And somewhere it stopped being a choice and started being... necessary.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And I kept thinking like, I can stop whenever, this isn't a big deal, but then... detox happened and I was like, oh. Oh, that's... that's bad. That's actually bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a moment in there — 'oh, that's actually bad' — where something shifted for you. What does that feel like now, sitting with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Scary. Like... I'm sixteen. I'm sixteen and I just went to detox and I don't — what does that mean for me? Like, is this just... is this my life now? Am I gonna be this person forever? Because I don't want that. I really don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. I want to say something clearly: no. This is not your life sentence. At sixteen, going through what you just went through, being in this chair and saying out loud 'I don't want that' — that matters more than you know. You came in here today ready to fight me and instead you just told me something really true about yourself. That's not the profile of someone who's destined to stay stuck.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I thought you were gonna be like, annoying. Like some clipboard guy telling me about the dangers of alcohol or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I do have a clipboard. I just hid it because I knew you'd hate it. Look — let me pull together what I'm hearing: you didn't come here by choice, you're angry about what feels like a double standard at home, and at the same time something inside you genuinely got scared during detox. And that fear? That's actually the part of you that wants something different. I'd like to keep meeting with you — not to fix you, but to figure out together what 'different' could actually look like. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Um... yeah, okay. I think I can do that.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Welcome back. I just want to say — coming back for a second session, that means something. A lot of people don't make it back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... I said I'd come back, so. [pause] I keep my word. At least I've got that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's been on your mind since we last spoke?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Same stuff, I guess. It's been a rough week. My ex is trying to change the visitation schedule again, so I've been... I mean, I had a few more drinks than I probably should've. But that's just — the stress has been a lot, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So right when you're trying to find your footing, she changes the ground under you again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly! I mean, what am I supposed to do? She just — she does whatever she wants and I'm just supposed to sit there and take it? So yeah, I had some drinks. Sue me. That's not a crime.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say you had some drinks this week — what does a rough week look like for you lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, like... five, six beers a night maybe. More on weekends. But I'm not like, falling down drunk. I go to work every single day. I'm functional. That's not — that's not the same as having a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want me to know you're still holding things together. And I hear that. I also hear something else underneath it — it sounds like it's just... exhausting. Carrying all of this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [long pause] Yeah. Yeah, it is. I get home and the place is just — it's so goddamn quiet. The kids used to be there every other week, and now she's talking about moving them further away, and I just... I don't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're still showing up for them even when everything around you is falling apart. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I try to. I don't know if I'm doing a good job of it though. My oldest — she's sixteen — she called me last week and I could just tell, you know, she was worried about me. And that... that hit different. That hit hard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like to hear that from her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Awful. She shouldn't — she shouldn't have to worry about me. I'm the parent. I'm supposed to be the one who... [voice breaks] I'm not doing a great job of that lately. I really haven't been.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. You came back today because you keep your word — that's who you are. You're holding down a job, you're trying to stay in your kids' lives. And at the same time, the drinking has gotten heavier since the divorce, the house feels empty in a way that's hard to sit with, and your daughter's worry cut right through you. There's a lot of pain underneath all of this anger.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [quietly] Yeah. That's... yeah. I didn't — I haven't thought of it all laid out like that but. Yeah. That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you think about your daughter — about the dad you want to be for her — what comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want her to not have to worry about me. I want to be the guy I was before all this. I used to coach her soccer team, you know? We'd go get breakfast after games, just the two of us. I want... I want that back. I don't know if I can have it back, but I want it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That wanting — that pull back toward who you've been for her — that's still in there. That didn't go away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't. [pause] ...Maybe that's why I actually came back. I don't know. Maybe I need to — maybe I actually need to do something about this.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this wasn't exactly your idea, and I want to acknowledge that upfront. Before we get into anything, I just want to understand — what's your sense of why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My coach and the school counselor basically made me come, so... yeah. I don't think I actually need to be here. Like, I'm fine. They're just — they're making a way bigger deal out of this than it is. And honestly I've done this before, the counseling thing, and it didn't do anything, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this feels like their idea, not yours. You got pushed into a room you didn't ask to walk into — and you've been in rooms like this before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, I get it, everyone's worried, whatever. But I'm not — I'm not some alcoholic. That's not what this is. I go out on weekends, I have fun, that's what college is. Everyone does it. Why am I the one sitting in an office?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The word 'alcoholic' really doesn't fit for you. And I'm not here to argue that label. I'm curious though — your coach got involved, which is pretty significant. What did he actually say to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He basically said I'm benched if things don't turn around. Which is — I mean, that's not fair. It was the off-season, everyone was partying. I wasn't doing anything different from anyone else on the team. He just singled me out because my numbers dipped, and that's... that could be anything. That could be fatigue, bad matchups, whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your spot on the team is on the line. That's not a small thing — and you're sitting here feeling like the blame is landing on you unfairly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Because — look, I work hard. People don't see that. I'm in the weight room, I'm at every practice, I do everything I'm supposed to. And then one bad stretch and suddenly I'm the problem. It's like... I don't know, it feels like no one actually sees the work I put in.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You work hard. That's real, and it clearly matters a lot to you — being someone who shows up and puts in the effort. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Obviously. Like, that's why I'm even at this school. I got recruited. I have a scholarship. It's not like I'm just here messing around, this is... yeah. This is everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that — what the scholarship actually means to you. Not just the basketball part, but what it represents.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm the first person in my family to get something like this. My mom... she doesn't have a lot, and I was supposed to be the one who like, figures it out. Makes something happen. And now I'm — I'm potentially throwing that away to go out on weekends and drink with guys who are gonna forget me the second I'm off the team. That's... that's actually kind of embarrassing to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage to say. You're carrying something much bigger than basketball — you're carrying your family's story in this. And you're starting to connect what's been happening on weekends to where things are heading.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to lose my spot. I really don't. And... I know my numbers are down, I know my coach barely looks at me in practice anymore. I knew something had to change, I just — I didn't want to admit that to like, a stranger in an office. You know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something had to change. That's your thought. Not your coach's, not the counselor's. Yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, it's not like I'm out there having the time of my life every weekend either. Honestly I mostly just go along with it because it's easier than being the one guy who stays home. But I wake up Monday and I feel like garbage, and practice is brutal, and I'm like... why did I even do that. So. Yeah, I guess I knew.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You have a scholarship that means everything — for you and for your family. You're someone who works hard and needs that to be recognized. But lately there's been a drift, and you can feel it in your body, in your performance, in your coach's eyes. You're not even really enjoying the weekends anymore. And there's this tension — between keeping up with your social world and holding onto the thing you actually came here for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah, that's it. I never really laid it out like that before. When you say it out loud it sounds kind of obvious, doesn't it? Like — why was I even fighting this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — looking forward — what would it look like for you to actually hold onto both things? Your friendships, your place on the team, your family's investment in you. Is there a version where those aren't all pulling in different directions?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... maybe? Like I don't have to drink every time we go out. I've never actually tried just... not doing it. I always kind of assumed it would be weird or whatever. But maybe it wouldn't be. I don't know, maybe that's a start. I don't know.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, welcome. I'm Marcus. Fair warning upfront — no ink blots, no couch, and I promise I won't ask you how your relationship with your mother is. You can actually relax in here. What's your name?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh — Jake. Yeah. I've never, like... I've never done this before so I don't really know what I'm supposed to say or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No script needed, seriously. So what brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My coach basically... okay, look. He thinks I have a drinking problem. Which I don't. I'm in college, everyone drinks. He looked at my stats and just — I don't know, jumped to conclusions. He said I either come talk to someone or I lose my starting spot so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the way you see it, this is really more about your coach's concerns than something you came in worried about yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I mean — okay, I'll be honest, I've had some rough practices lately. And there was a game last month that wasn't great. But that's not all drinking. There's other stuff going on too. Stress, school, whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about that game. What was happening for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: We had a party the night before and I just... I didn't sleep. I could feel it the whole game, like my legs were just gone. And then coach pulled me in the third quarter and I'm sitting on the bench and I'm like... that's never happened to me. Not once. I've started every single game since sophomore year of high school.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real record you built. That doesn't happen by accident — that's years of work. And sitting on that bench for the first time... that must've hit pretty hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't let myself feel it at the time, I just kind of laughed it off with the guys after. But yeah. Sitting there watching... I kept thinking, this is not me. Like, this is not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Who are you, then? As an athlete.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm the guy who works harder than everyone else. Like — I was up at 5am all through high school, I turned down other scholarships because this program was the best fit for me. I care. I actually really care about this. That's the thing that's messing with me because it's like... why am I acting like I don't?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this version of you — the one who's up at 5am, who made real sacrifices to get here, who chose this program because it mattered — and then there's what's been happening lately. And it sounds like those two are starting to feel pretty far apart from each other.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. That's kind of it, actually. I don't know when that changed. The parties just became the thing everyone does and I never really — I never stopped to ask myself if it was worth it. I just went along.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you — personally, not for your coach — if things just kept going the way they've been going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd lose everything, probably. My scholarship. My spot. And I only have two more seasons. Two. That's it and then it's just... over. I can party in my thirties if I want to. What am I even doing right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That right there — that's real clarity. You can see the math. And I want to point something out: I haven't convinced you of anything. That was already in you when you walked in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I just needed to say it out loud. My teammates aren't gonna get it — they'd think I was being dramatic or whatever. But yeah. I do want to turn this around. I actually do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you came in today thinking your coach was overreacting, and somewhere along the way you found something that was already yours — two seasons left, a record you built from 5am mornings, and a pretty clear sense of who you actually want to be. I'm not going to tell you what to do with that. But I am curious: what feels like one realistic thing you could do differently? Not a total overhaul — just something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... being more intentional? Like, not swearing off everything, but being the one who decides instead of just going along with whatever. I think I can actually do that. And I don't know, I feel a little better which is honestly not what I was expecting when I came in here.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So I hear this was not exactly on your calendar this morning. I'm Sanjay — I work here at the center. You didn't have to come in, and you did, so I appreciate that. What's your name?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Margaret. And no, it was not on my calendar. My daughter-in-law dropped me off like I was some kind of... I don't even know. I don't really know what I'm supposed to be doing here, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Well, Margaret, since you're here — what would you say is going on, from your perspective? Not your daughter-in-law's, not anyone else's. Yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: From my perspective, nothing is going on. I have pain — I've had pain for years, my back, my hips — and the medication the doctor gives me doesn't always do enough. So sometimes I have a glass of wine in the evening. Maybe two. It helps me sleep. I don't see what the big fuss is about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The wine fills a gap that the medication leaves. And meanwhile, everyone around you is treating this like some kind of crisis.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes! Exactly. They're acting like I'm — I don't know — falling down drunk all day. I'm not. I raised three children. I've been running my own household since before my daughter-in-law was born. I'm a grown woman and I think I know my own body better than anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been managing your own life for a long time, and now it feels like everyone's suddenly decided you can't be trusted with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yes. That is exactly what it feels like. It's humiliating. Coming in here like I'm some kind of — some kind of problem to be dealt with. They took the bottles out of my house, you know. My own house.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about the nights. When the medication isn't enough — what does that actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Some nights it just... it doesn't touch it. The pain. And I'm lying there at two in the morning and I can't call my son — he has work, he has his kids. So I'd get up and... I'd have a drink. And now they've taken that away and I don't — I don't know what I'm supposed to do instead. I'm scared, honestly. I haven't said that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You found the one thing that got you through those nights alone... and now it's gone, and you don't have anything to replace it yet. That's a frightening place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I keep thinking — what happens when the pain gets worse? Because it will. I'm 72. I'm not going to get better. And I... I don't want to fall apart in front of everyone. I don't want to become a burden. My husband, Harold, he was very sick at the end and my son gave up so much. I can't do that to them. I can't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you — not being a burden? If you could say more about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It means... everything, I think. I want to still be someone they come to, not someone they have to look after. I want to be useful. I want them to still — I don't know — I want them to still want to be around me, not out of obligation. That sounds terrible to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound terrible at all. What I'm hearing is that everything you've been doing — managing alone, the wine at two in the morning, not calling your son — all of it has been about love. Protecting them.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I hadn't thought of it that way. I just thought I was being stubborn. My son would probably agree with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I reflect back what I've been hearing from you today? You've been living with serious pain for years, managing it almost entirely alone because you love your family too much to lean on them. You've been scared — about the future, about losing your independence — and you've been sitting with that fear by yourself at two in the morning. That is an enormous amount to carry, Margaret. And I want to say — the fact that you walked in here today, even when you didn't want to, tells me something about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... maybe I have been trying too hard to do this alone. Maybe that hasn't been helping anyone, least of all me. I don't know if I'm ready to call myself — I mean, I'm not an alcoholic. But maybe... maybe there's something here worth talking about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not as a problem. As someone who deserves to not be in pain alone at two in the morning. What would it look like to you — getting some support that actually worked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... if there's something that could actually help with the pain at night, so I'm not choosing between calling my son or having a drink — I'd try it. I really would. I'm not too proud to try. I just didn't know there was anything to try.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for coming in today, Gerald. I know this is your first session after completing the program, and... that takes real courage. I just want you to know there's no agenda here — we can go at whatever pace feels right for you. So, how are you feeling as you walk in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't... I mean, I'm here, right? That's something. I don't know, I feel like I'm being processed through some kind of system. Detox, now this. My old supervisor set this whole thing up and I just — I'm not angry, I'm just... tired of explaining myself to people.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tired of explaining yourself. Like you've been having to justify who you are to a lot of people lately.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I worked for that company for thirty-one years. Thirty-one years without so much as a written warning. And then I retire and six months later they're sending me to treatment like I'm some kind of — I don't know. It just stings a little, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thirty-one years. That's a long time of showing up and doing things right. And now you're in a position that feels... unfair, maybe? I'm curious — when you think back to that incident that led to this referral, what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had a few drinks before I went in to clear out my old office. It was a Saturday, nobody was supposed to be there. I just... I couldn't face doing it sober, you know? Thirty-one years of your life in cardboard boxes. And then Karen from HR walks in and — look, I wasn't falling down drunk. I was sad. There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You needed something to help you get through an incredibly painful moment. Packing up thirty-one years of your life — that's a real loss, Gerald. And somewhere in you, you knew that was going to be hard to face on your own.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, I did know that. I knew it the night before. I was sitting in my kitchen at like two in the morning thinking about it and I just — I started drinking then, actually. Not the next day. The night before. I haven't really told anyone that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for trusting me with that. Sitting alone at two in the morning... what's been life like for you since you retired? Before the incident, in those quieter moments at home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Quiet. Very quiet. My wife passed four years ago, so it's just me and the dog now, and Biscuit's getting old too so he sleeps most of the day. I thought retirement was going to be — you know, golf and traveling. But my knees aren't great and I don't really have anyone to travel with. So it's just... a lot of daytime television and waiting for it to get dark so I can go to bed. The drinking kind of filled the hours, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Waiting for it to get dark so you can go to bed. That's such an honest thing to say, and it sounds incredibly lonely, Gerald. Like the days stretch out with nothing to anchor them.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's a good way to put it. Nothing to anchor them. I never thought I'd miss having somewhere to be, but I do. I miss — I miss mattering to something. Does that make sense? And I think that's when the drinking got... more than just a couple glasses of wine with dinner.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes complete sense. Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I've got it right. You spent thirty-one years with a clear purpose, a place where you mattered. Then retirement came — and instead of freedom, it felt more like... emptiness. Your wife isn't here. The days are long. And drinking became a way to fill that space, to get through the hours. And somewhere along the way, you noticed it had become something more than you intended.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My doctor said something about my liver. At my checkup in February. And I kind of just nodded along and drove home and poured myself a scotch. Which is — I know how that sounds. I just didn't want to think about it. But I'm thinking about it now. More than I'd like to admit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted when your doctor said that — even if you pushed it away at the time. What does it mean to you now, sitting here today, thinking about your health?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I have a daughter. In Portland. We're not — we don't talk as much as we should. But she called me when she found out about the detox and she was... she wasn't angry. She was scared. And I don't want to be someone my daughter is scared for. I want to — I want to be around for a while yet, I think. See if things can be different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to be around. You want to rebuild something with your daughter. That tells me there's a lot of life still ahead of you that matters to you, Gerald — even if it's been hard to see that from inside those long quiet days.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: You know what, yeah. Yeah, there is. I think — I think I'd been sort of waiting to die without really admitting that to myself. And that's... that's a terrible way to spend your time. I completed that detox program. I did it. I didn't think I would, but I did. So maybe I can do this too.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You did do it. That was all you. As we start to wind down today, I'm wondering — if you imagine the next few weeks, what's one small thing that might help the days feel a little less like something to get through?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There's a — at the library, there's a group on Thursday mornings. For seniors. I drove past the sign about a hundred times and never went in. I think maybe I'll go in this week. Just to see. And I'm going to call my daughter tonight. I've been putting that off, but I'm going to do it tonight.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you came in today. I know it's not always easy to walk through that door. There's no agenda here, no checklist we have to get through. I just want to understand a little about what's been going on for you... whatever you feel comfortable sharing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... my sister basically said she wouldn't stop calling me until I came in, so. Here I am. I've done the therapy thing before. Didn't really... I don't know. Didn't stick.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because someone who loves you pushed a little, and another part of you has some real doubts about whether this is going to be any different from before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah, that's pretty much it. Last time I was in therapy, the guy kept wanting me to talk about my childhood and... I don't know, that's not really what's going on with me. I just — I get dark sometimes. And drinking takes the edge off. I don't think that makes me an alcoholic or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like that last experience left you feeling kind of dismissed, like you weren't being heard on what actually matters to you right now. I'm curious — when you say you get dark sometimes... what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... just, nothing feels worth it. You know? I'll be fine for a few days and then it just — crashes. And then I can't sleep, I can't think straight, I'm useless at work... my wife — well, ex-wife — she used to say I'd disappear inside myself. Um. I don't really talk about this stuff. It feels weird saying it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet you just did. That took something. ... The way you describe it — crashing, going dark, disappearing — that sounds exhausting to carry around. And the drinking helps you get through those times.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It — yeah, it does. For a few hours at least. And then... I don't know, I wake up the next morning and I feel worse, and I know that, I'm not stupid. But in the moment it's like — what else am I supposed to do? It's the only thing that quiets it down. That scares me a little, honestly. That I can't think of anything else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not stupid — you know exactly what it's doing and what it costs you the next morning. And still, in that moment, it feels like the only door you've got. What would it mean for you if there were other doors?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I mean. I'd probably sleep better. Maybe my daughter wouldn't look at me the way she does. She's twelve and she's already... she's already figured it out. What's going on. Kids know. And I hate that. I hate that she knows.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The look on her face. That stays with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it does. She doesn't — she doesn't say anything, she's a good kid. But she gets quiet when I've been drinking. Pulls back. And I think... I think I'm teaching her something, and I don't want to be teaching her that. That this is just how men deal with things. My dad did the same thing and I swore I wasn't going to be that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in here skeptical, maybe half-ready to walk back out. And in the same breath you're talking about the man you want to be for your daughter. The gap between those two things — that sounds like it weighs on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. More than anything, honestly. The drinking, the depression, whatever... I could maybe live with all that. But I can't — I don't want her to grow up and have this picture of me in her head. As somebody who just... gave up. I haven't given up. I don't think I have. I just don't know what I'm supposed to do instead.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That matters. That's worth holding onto. ... If you think back to a time, maybe even just a day, where the darkness was there but you didn't reach for a drink — what was different about that day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hm. ... There was this one Saturday last fall, I took Maya — my daughter — to one of her soccer games. And I was having a rough week. But I was there, on the sideline, and she scored a goal and she ran over to me, not her mom, me. And I wasn't thinking about any of it. The drinking, the... any of it. Just her. I went home and I cooked dinner and I didn't drink that night. First time in a while. I forgot about that actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I've heard, because I think it's important. You came in today reluctant, having been burned before. You carry a depression that crashes down on you, and you've been using alcohol to survive those crashes — you know the cost but it's felt like the only option. And underneath all of that is a father who hasn't given up, who remembers a Saturday in the fall where he was exactly the dad he wants to be. And that memory — you'd almost forgotten it was there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... I don't know. It doesn't sound as hopeless as it feels inside my head. Like there's actually something there to work with. I wasn't expecting to feel like that when I walked in here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There is something there. There really is. ... What would it mean to you, to come back next week and keep pulling on that thread?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I want to try. I mean actually try this time. Not just show up. Maya deserves that. And maybe I do too, I don't know. Yeah. I'll come back.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. Last time we talked you'd set a few things you wanted to try out during the week. Before we get into all that — how are you doing today, just overall?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here, right? That's something. Honestly the week was rough but I'm not — look, I'm managing. I always manage. That's kind of what I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up, and that counts. And it sounds like the week threw some things at you that were hard to deal with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Had a thing happen Thursday night. My wife — we got into it again. She found a bottle I had out in the garage. I told her it was just for when the guys come over, you know? It's not like I was hiding it from her. It was right there on the shelf.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was that night like for you — when she found it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Annoying. Because she makes it this whole dramatic thing. Every other house in our neighborhood the husbands have beer in the fridge, they got a bar cart in the living room, whatever. Nobody's getting interrogated about it. I did two deployments. I think I've earned a damn drink at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've carried a lot — two deployments, coming back, trying to hold things together at home — and it feels like you're being held to a different standard than the people around you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like I'm the problem, right? When half the guys I served with drink way more than me. I'm functional. I go to work, I pay the bills, I show up to my kid's stuff. What more do people want from me? Like at what point is it enough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot of pieces and keeping them in the air — work, bills, being present for your kid. That's real. And I'm also noticing you used the word 'rough' to describe this week. I want to make sure I understand what that word means for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said... she actually used the word this time. Divorce. She's thrown it out before but this time she had this look. Like she wasn't — it didn't feel like a threat. It felt like she'd already kind of... I don't know. Made up her mind about something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That landed differently. Like something had shifted in how she said it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I just... I sat there. I didn't yell, I didn't argue. I just sat there and finished the rest of the bottle. Which — I know how that looks. I know. I'm not... I'm not an idiot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You knew in that moment something wasn't right, and you're still sitting with that now. What does it mean to you — actually losing her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's... she's the only person who still sees me as just me. Not as like a veteran, not as some project to fix. Just Marcus. And my daughter — she's seven. She completely adores me, man. And I keep thinking, if this falls apart... what does she remember? Dad who always had a drink in his hand? That's not — that's not who I want to be to her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — the dad your daughter carries with her — that means something to you. That's not a small thing, Marcus.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No it's not. I just... I don't — I was raised that you handle your own stuff. In the military you handle your own stuff or you're a liability. But maybe... I don't know. Maybe this is a different kind of thing. Maybe it's not about being weak.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You had a hard week — a real confrontation with your wife, and this time it hit differently than before. You came in today anyway. And when you think about what actually matters most to you — your daughter, your wife, the kind of man you want them to see — that's where things get clearest for you. Is that close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I think I needed to hear it laid out like that. Because in my head it's all just noise, you know? But when you say it back like that it's like — okay. There's something here that's actually worth fighting for.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you just said — what feels like one thing, even something small, that you'd want to do differently before we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I want to actually tell her. Tell my wife I heard her. Not just like — not just apologize and move on. Actually tell her I'm trying to figure this out for real. And maybe get that bottle out of the garage. I know that sounds small but it's like... it's something I can actually do today. That's a start, right?

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — telehealth. I have to say, doing this from your home office probably beats a waiting room full of magazines from 2019. I'm Dr. Marcus. Before we get into anything heavy, how are you actually doing right now? Like, genuinely.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm fine. I mean... I'm here because I have to be. My lawyer said it'd look better for the case, so. Here I am. Sitting in my home office on a Thursday afternoon talking to a stranger instead of running my company.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Court-mandated therapy — not exactly how most people plan their Thursdays. I get it. So I'd rather not waste your time with a bunch of intake-form questions. What happened, from your perspective? What brought you to this point?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My perspective is I had one bad night, made a stupid call — literally — and now I'm jumping through hoops. I don't have a drinking problem. I have a stress problem. Four hundred employees, a board that second-guesses every move I make, investors who want results yesterday. The scotch helps me decompress. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A bottle a night to decompress. That's... a lot of decompressing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Do you know what I deal with in a day? By the time I sit down at night the scotch is the only thing that actually turns my brain off. And it doesn't affect my work — my numbers have never been better. So. I don't really see what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your work performance — you're genuinely proud of that, and I believe you. But you mentioned a partner. You two are still together?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Technically. She moved into the guest room... three months ago. She doesn't say anything anymore, she just — she looks at me sometimes like she's already grieving something. And I don't know how to... I built everything for her. For us. And I don't know how to fix that. I don't even know where to start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Watching someone you love look at you like you're already gone — and not knowing how to reach them. That's a heavy thing to carry around every day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I come home to my own house and I'm... alone. What's the point of any of it? The company, the — all of it. I just come home and I pour a drink because what else am I going to do. There's no one waiting. There's nothing. ... I don't see a way through this, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to make sure I heard that — you don't see a way through. Not just the drinking. Through any of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not saying I'm going to stop drinking. I want to be clear. I've tried cutting back before — a few times actually — and it never sticks. Week, maybe two, then I'm right back. So I don't... I mean, what's the point of trying again. I don't think I can.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've tried before. More than once. There's a part of you that's wanted something different — otherwise you wouldn't have tried at all. What did those weeks feel like, when you were cutting back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It felt... lighter. Clearer. I had a dream — first time in years I actually remembered a dream. That was strange. But then the anxiety just comes back like a freight train and I don't have another... I don't have another gear. I never learned one. Nobody taught me how to deal with any of this without just pushing through it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing — tell me if I've got it wrong. You're someone who built something real, who has actually tried to change this before, more than once. And somewhere in there is a guy who remembered a dream, felt lighter, got a glimpse of something different. And right now you're sitting with the fear that you don't have the tools to get back there. That you'd just be setting yourself up to fail again. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... God, that's a lot more depressing when someone else says it. ... But yeah. That's about right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You remembered a dream. That's actually not a small thing — for someone drinking heavily for years, that's the brain starting to come back online. What do you think you'd need to feel like you weren't doing it alone this time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Last time I white-knuckled it by myself. Didn't tell anyone. Maybe — maybe if there was actual support. I don't know what that looks like exactly but... if I wasn't just grinding through it alone. Maybe that would be different. Maybe I'd be willing to actually try something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That 'maybe' is doing a lot of work right now, and I want you to hear this — you came in here today not wanting to be here, and you just said out loud that you don't want to do this alone anymore. That's a completely different conversation than the one we started with. What would one small step look like? Just one. Something that doesn't feel impossible.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I could... tell her. Tonight. That I'm thinking about it. She doesn't need to know everything but — she should know that I'm not just... sitting in here not caring. That might be a start. It might be too late. I don't know. But... maybe it's not.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time today, Marcus. I know this wasn't exactly your idea, so... I just want you to know there's no agenda here. We can go at whatever pace feels right for you. What's it like, being here right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's... look, I'm only here because Sandra basically gave me an ultimatum. So. I don't really see the point of this. No offense. I've talked to guys who went through therapy after they got back and it didn't do jack for most of them. I'm fine. I function. I go to work, I come home, I'm not out doing anything crazy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here for Sandra. And part of you is already bracing for this to be a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Pretty much. I mean — look, I drink. Okay? I'll just say it. But so does every guy I served with. You come back from two tours, you drink. That's just — that's what it is. It's not some disorder. It's not a disease. It's Tuesday, you crack a beer, big deal. I don't know why everyone's acting like I'm some... like I'm falling apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking was part of the culture. Part of how you and the guys held it together. I don't want to take that away from you or pretend I understand what those deployments were like. Can I ask — what was it like when you first got back? That transition home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... weird. Everything was just — weird. Like everyone's walking around worried about, I don't know, traffic and their fantasy football team and I'm sitting there like... I don't even know how to explain it. You feel like a ghost. Like you're watching everything through glass. And yeah, having a few drinks at night kind of... it turned the volume down, you know? Made it easier to sleep. That's not addiction. That's just coping.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Watching everything through glass. That's... that's a really vivid way to put it. Like you came back but something didn't quite come back with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Something like that. I don't — I don't really talk about that. Sandra thinks I just don't want to talk to her but it's not — it's not that simple. Some of it I can't even put into words. And when I try, I just get frustrated and then she gets upset and then I just — I go to the garage. Have a drink. It's easier than fighting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying something that doesn't have words. And instead of fighting with Sandra, you protect her from it. That's not nothing, Marcus.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm not trying to protect her. I just — I don't want to dump all my crap on her. She's got her own stuff. She works, she takes care of Eli — that's our son, he's seven — she does a lot. I know that. I'm not an idiot. I just... I don't know how to be the husband she needs right now. And drinking doesn't help that, I know that, okay, I'm not saying it does. I'm just saying it's not the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said you're not the husband she needs right now. What does that feel like to sit with?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It feels like... like I failed. Like I was supposed to come back and be — I don't know — better. More present. And instead I came back and it's like I'm less here than when I was deployed. At least then there was a reason I wasn't around. Now I'm right there in the same house and... Eli asked Sandra last month why Daddy always smells funny. And she told me that and I just... I didn't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: ... Eli noticed. And that landed differently than anything Sandra said.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. I can argue with Sandra. I've been doing that for years, we're good at that. But Eli... he doesn't — he's seven. He just says what he sees. And what he sees is his dad coming home and going straight to the garage. And I don't — I don't want him to remember me like that. I really don't. That scares me more than anything Sandra said.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came home from deployment carrying something you can't fully put into words. Drinking helped you manage that — turn down the volume, sleep, not have to fight. But somewhere along the way, the thing that was helping started costing you. Sandra is at a breaking point. And now Eli — your seven-year-old — has noticed something, and that hit you in a way nothing else has. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. I didn't think about it like that all laid out. But yeah. I guess I always told myself I had it under control. And maybe I don't. I don't know. Maybe I've been telling myself I'm fine because it was easier than admitting I'm not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something to say. It really did. So let me ask you — and you don't have to have an answer right now — when you imagine being the dad Eli talks about when he grows up... what does that version of you look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He's... he's present. Like, actually there. Throwing the ball around in the yard, helping with homework, not — not checking out. I want him to know I'm solid. That he can count on me. My dad wasn't around much and I swore I wouldn't do that. And I'm kind of doing that. Not the same way, but... yeah. I don't want that for him. I don't want him growing up thinking his dad chose a bottle over him, because that's not — that's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's who you are. A father who doesn't want to repeat the wound. A man who's been holding something enormous, mostly alone, and who walked into this call today even when part of him didn't want to. That matters. And I think you already know something needs to shift — not because Sandra said so, but because Eli deserves that version of you. And so do you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I think I've known for a while. I just didn't want to admit it because then I'd have to actually do something about it. But yeah. I'm — I don't know what that looks like yet. But I'm willing to figure it out. I think.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in... make yourself comfortable. I'm really glad you came today. This space is kind of yours — there's no agenda I'm pushing. Before we get into anything, I'm just curious: what would make today feel at least a little worth it for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... honestly? I don't know. My school counselor basically said I had to come here or there'd be like, consequences. So. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this really wasn't your idea.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. Not even a little. And like... I don't even think I did anything that wrong? Literally everyone was drinking at that thing. I just happened to be the one who got caught, and now I'm the one sitting in some office. It's kind of ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you're still trying to make sense of why you ended up here when others didn't. Can you walk me through what actually happened that night — just from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ugh. Okay. So it was after the homecoming game and people were just hanging out in the parking lot. Someone had drinks. I had like... two? Maybe two and a half, whatever. I wasn't even that drunk. And then Ms. Peterson walks by, sees me, and suddenly I'm the problem. Out of like fifteen other people.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That must have felt really unfair. Like you were singled out when so many other people were doing the exact same thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes! Exactly. Like I'm not exaggerating — there were so many people there and I'm the one who gets dragged into the counselor's office and now... this. I don't know. It just feels like I'm being made into some kind of example. And my parents found out, so that was a whole... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your parents finding out on top of everything else — that adds a whole other layer. I hear you. And I want you to know, I'm not here to pile on or make you into a problem. I'm just... I'd like to understand you a little better, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... okay. I guess. I just — I'm not an alcoholic or anything, if that's what this is about. I'm literally a normal eighteen-year-old.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not putting any label on you at all. I'm genuinely curious about something though — and you can answer however feels true. Setting aside what everyone else does... just thinking about you... what does drinking actually do for you? Like, what does it feel like at a party when you have a drink?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I don't know. It's like... social, I guess? It's just what you do. But also — okay, I actually get kind of nervous in big groups. Like genuinely anxious. And it helps with that. It makes it easier to just... be normal and talk to people without overthinking everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it quiets something down for you. The anxious part, the overthinking — and drinking gives you a way to just be in the moment with people.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Which... I know how that sounds. And I've kind of noticed that lately it's been happening more? Like not just at big parties but even smaller things. Like a few friends just hanging out and I'll still want a drink just to feel okay. That's kind of... I don't know. That's kind of new.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You noticed that shift yourself. That's not nothing — a lot of people wouldn't even let themselves see that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my best friend kind of said something to me a couple months ago. Made a comment about it. And I just brushed it off because I didn't want to deal with it. But sitting here saying it out loud I'm like... maybe she had a point. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just gently pull together what I've heard. You came in feeling like this whole situation was unfair — and that part makes complete sense. And underneath all of that, you're noticing something yourself: that drinking has been filling a role around anxiety, and that it's been creeping into more situations lately. And there's someone who cares about you who saw something too, even if it was hard to hear at the time. That's a lot of things pointing in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... when you put it like that. I don't want to need it, you know? Like I don't want to be the person who can't handle a social thing without drinking first. That's not... that's not who I want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's really important — the person you want to be. What would it look like, do you think, if you figured out how to handle that anxiety without needing a drink first?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'd feel more like myself, honestly. Like I'm actually pretty outgoing when I'm comfortable with people — it's just the in-between part that's hard. Maybe if I could actually deal with the anxiety stuff for real... like actually talk to someone about it... I think I'd be okay. Maybe. I think that's actually something I'd want to try.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for joining today. I know you're at home, so hopefully that's a little easier than coming into an office. I want to be straight with you from the start — I know you're here because the court ordered it, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. So before we get into anything structured, what's going through your mind right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What's going through my mind. Are you serious right now? I'm sitting in my own house, being forced to talk to some therapist on a laptop screen, because of a — look, this whole thing is a joke, okay? The system is designed to squeeze guys like me and this is just another hoop. So. Let's just get through it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're furious. Being here feels completely unjust.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, it does. I blew a .09, man. Point-oh-nine. Legal limit's .08. That is — that's basically nothing. My coworker drives home at a .13 every Friday and nobody bats an eye. But because I had one bad night a couple years back, they're watching me, and now I get the second offense treatment like I'm some kind of... like I'm dangerous. I'm not dangerous. I went to work this morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about that night — what actually happened, from your side of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What happened is I went out with some guys from work, had a few beers, waited — I sat there for like two, two and a half hours. I wasn't swerving. I wasn't speeding. I got pulled over because of a broken taillight. A taillight. And then they smell alcohol and suddenly it's this whole production. I thought I did everything... mostly right. And I still ended up here, twice now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you tried to be responsible — you waited, you weren't driving erratically — and it still went sideways on you. That must feel like no matter what you do, you can't win.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes. Thank you. And now my ex — she's using this in the custody thing, which is a whole other disaster. I go to work every day, I pay my taxes, I show up for my kids on my weekends. I don't bother anybody. And this is... this is what I get for it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a lot on the line here — custody, your record, your time. What does a normal week look like for you when it comes to drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Normal. Like... normal. I have a beer or two after work, maybe more on weekends when the kids aren't with me. That's how I unwind, that's how everyone I know unwinds. My dad drank, my uncles drank. I'm not sitting there pounding vodka at noon. It's just... it's what adults do after a long day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're dealing with a court case, a custody fight, and you still showed up today and you're engaging with me, even if it's under protest. That actually takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's not like I had a choice. [pause] But yeah. I'm not trying to lose my license, lose time with my kids. That's — that's the last thing I want. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your kids keep coming up. They clearly matter a lot to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [sighs] They're everything, honestly. I've got a nine-year-old and a six-year-old. The little one doesn't really get what's going on, but my older one... she heard Karen and me arguing about all this. She knows something's wrong. She asked me if I was going to jail. And I just — I don't want her carrying that around, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your daughter's asking if you're going to jail. What goes through you when you picture that conversation?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I feel like garbage. I do. [pause] I still don't think I have like, a drinking problem. I want to be clear about that. But, if someone asked me honestly... I'd probably say I drink more than I should some nights. Especially when I'm stressed. Like, when the custody stuff flares up, or work is bad, I... yeah. I reach for it pretty fast.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty to say. There's a part of you that's noticed stress and drinking have gotten kind of... linked together.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Maybe. I'm not gonna have some big moment here, I want to be upfront about that. But yeah, I guess. When things are bad, I don't — I don't call somebody, I don't go to the gym. I just... pour a drink. And it's faster than it used to be. Like the threshold got lower somewhere and I didn't really notice until just now saying it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You came in angry — and that makes sense, because this was forced on you and it feels deeply unfair. At the same time, there are people in your life, especially your kids, who matter more to you than pretty much anything. And underneath all of this, there's a part of you that's starting to notice that stress and drinking have gotten more tangled up than maybe you'd want. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — I mean, I'm still not happy about being here. But that's... that's pretty much it, yeah.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this isn't exactly how you planned to spend your Thursday afternoon. I'm just wondering — what's it been like for you, getting here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Kind of weird. I've been in clinics before, like, for regular checkups and stuff, but... I don't know. I'm just here because I have to be. The court said I needed to come, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here, and part of you is still figuring out what this even is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... I'm not some, like, alcoholic or whatever. I just — I made a mistake. One night, one bad decision, and now I'm sitting in a therapist's office. It's just a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that night, if you're comfortable. What was going on for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was at a work happy hour. We do these, like, every other week — it's practically mandatory for marketing. And I had a few drinks and I thought I was fine. Everyone drinks at these things, my whole team does. I just... I got unlucky, I guess. Wrong place, wrong time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking felt completely normal — it's just what happens at those events. And yet here you are, dealing with consequences that feel really out of proportion to what you thought was just a regular night out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And it's embarrassing, honestly. My parents don't even know — I told them it was a minor traffic thing. I just... I don't want people thinking I have some kind of problem, because I don't. I work hard, I'm good at my job. This doesn't define me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your reputation — how people see you — that clearly matters a lot to you.

utterances.speaker: client
