utterances.text: Of course it does. I've worked my ass off to get where I am. I'm 28 and I'm already managing campaigns for three major accounts. I don't need people looking at me like I'm some kind of... mess. Because I'm not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something real. And at the same time, I'm hearing that there's a part of this — the DUI, keeping it from your parents — that's been sitting heavy on you. Even if it was just one night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. It's stressful. I haven't been sleeping great. I keep thinking about what would have happened if — like, what if there had been someone in the road, you know? That's the part that actually scares me. But I still don't think that means I have a drinking problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That thought — what could have happened — it's been with you. What does it bring up when it surfaces?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Guilt, I guess? Like... I pride myself on being responsible. I'm the one who has everything together. And then I — I wasn't. That night I wasn't. And I hate that about myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real honesty to sit with. You care deeply about being someone who shows up responsibly — at work, in your life. And that night created a gap between who you see yourself as and what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's actually exactly it. I've just been staying busy, pushing it down, but it's there. I don't know if my drinking is a 'problem' problem, but I think maybe I need to look at it more honestly than I have been.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would looking at it more honestly look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... being more aware of how much I'm drinking at those work things. Not just doing it on autopilot. I like having a good time, I'm not going to pretend I don't, but I also don't want to be the person who doesn't know when to stop. I don't want another night like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I've heard from you today. You came in feeling like this was something you had to do, not something you wanted. And over the last hour, you've talked about the pressure at those work events, how much your sense of responsibility and your reputation matter to you, and that moment — imagining what could have gone differently that night. And somewhere in all of that, a part of you started to wonder whether paying closer attention to your drinking might actually be worth doing. Not because something is broken in you, but because you care about the kind of person you want to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yeah. I still don't think I'm like, an alcoholic. But I'm willing to — I don't know — actually think about it. Maybe come back. See where this goes.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time to come in today — I know you mentioned you're between classes, so I want to make sure we use our time well. To start, I'm just curious... what brought you here today, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, honestly? My mom kind of... pushed me to come. She visited last weekend and I think she was just — she noticed some things and got worried. I don't know, I figured I'd at least show up and see what this was about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you showed up. That matters — even when someone else is the one who suggested it, you still made the choice to walk through that door. What do you think she noticed that had her concerned?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... probably the drinking. I've been — okay so third year of my PhD has been brutal. Like, genuinely brutal. My advisor basically told me last month that my last two chapters were 'not up to standard,' and I just... I started having a few drinks at night to like, decompress? And I guess it's become more than a few. She saw the bottles when she was helping me clean up and kind of freaked out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a really heavy few months — the pressure from your advisor, the feedback on your work, and then trying to find some way to get through the evenings. And now your mom's worried on top of all that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it's been a lot. And the thing is, I know I'm not — like, I'm not some alcoholic, you know? I'm just stressed. Every grad student I know drinks. It's basically the culture. But I guess... I don't know, it's gotten to where I'm like, looking forward to it in a way that kind of scares me a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about how much you're looking forward to it is giving you pause.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like it's — okay, I'll just say it. Sometimes I'll be in the middle of trying to write and I'll just be like, counting down to when I can have a drink. And then I have one and I feel better for like an hour and then I feel worse and then I have another one. And then it's 2am and I've written nothing and I feel like garbage. And then I wake up the next day and I'm behind again and the whole cycle just... ugh.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking starts as a way to get relief, but by the end of the night it's actually made things harder — you're behind, you feel worse, and then tomorrow's already more stressful before it's even started. It's become part of the problem, not just a solution to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. When you put it like that it sounds obvious. I guess I knew that. I just — I didn't have anywhere else to put it, you know? The stress. I don't even know if I belong in this program. My advisor clearly thinks I'm mediocre. Half the people in my cohort seem so much more... together than me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feeling of not belonging — of looking around and thinking everyone else has it figured out — that's an incredibly painful place to be sitting in, especially when you're trying to produce creative intellectual work at the same time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's exhausting. I chose this program because I actually love my research. Like genuinely — I came in so excited. And now I just feel like... I don't know. Hollow? I haven't felt excited about my work in months. And that scares me more than anything, honestly. More than my advisor, more than my mom. Because if I lose that, what's the point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The love for your research — that's still in there. You just said it: you came in excited. That hasn't disappeared, it's buried under months of stress and exhaustion and a cycle that's been burning through your energy at night. Can I ask — when you imagine finishing this degree, actually getting to the other side of it, what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I want to do research. Real research, at a place where I have some autonomy. I want to publish work that actually matters. I've had this vision since undergrad of — okay this sounds dorky — but of having my own lab someday. Mentoring students. Contributing something real. That's why I'm here. That's always been why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That vision is still completely intact. And I want to reflect something back to you: you just described, in pretty clear terms, a pattern that's actively working against getting there — the late nights, the lost writing hours, waking up behind. You can see how it's in conflict with what you actually want.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I can see that. I think part of me has been... avoiding seeing that. Because if I admit it's a problem then I have to do something about it and I already feel like I have zero capacity. But yeah. It's in the way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real honesty to say. And I want to be clear — I'm not here to take away something that's been helping you survive a brutal stretch. I'm here to help you figure out what you actually want to do about it, if anything. So: what feels like one small thing that might be possible, given where you are right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... maybe I could try to — like, not go cold turkey or whatever, but maybe set a rule for myself. Like, not before 10pm. Or not on nights before I have a meeting with my advisor. Something that keeps it from eating into my actual work time. Because that's the part that's killing me. The morning-after fog.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today because someone who loves you was worried, and you leave having named something that's been costing you — your energy, your writing, your sense of yourself as a researcher. And you came up with a first step that fits your life. That's not nothing. I'd like to meet again and hear how that goes — and also start exploring some other ways to manage the pressure that don't have the morning-after cost. Would that be worth coming back for?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think so. I actually feel... a little lighter? Which is weird because nothing has changed yet. But yeah. I'll come back.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. How have things been since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Um... okay, mostly. I've been trying, like, I really have. I got back into the studio last week which felt good. But then... I don't know, I hit this wall and it all kind of fell apart again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You made it back to the studio — that's real. And then something shifted.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I sat down in front of the canvas and just... nothing. Total blank. And then of course my brain goes straight to — okay, you know what would help right now. And I did. I had a few glasses and I thought it would unlock something but I just ended up staring at the same blank canvas, except now I was also kind of dizzy. Which is, um... yeah. Not ideal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you went to the thing that's always felt like it should work — and this time it didn't deliver. What was that like, sitting there waiting for something that didn't come?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terrifying, honestly. Because drinking was always — it was my... I mean I built my whole identity around this idea that I'm the artist who works a certain way. Late nights, wine, music, and then things just flow. And if that's not true anymore, then what am I? I don't even know who I am without that ritual. It sounds so stupid when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. It sounds like you've been carrying something really heavy — this belief that your creativity and the drinking are inseparable. And now you're starting to wonder if that's actually been true.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I've been looking at my old work. From before. Like, five, six years ago. And it's better. It's so much better and I— god, I used to barely drink back then. I thought I was just less experienced, less bold or whatever. But now I'm wondering if I had it backwards the whole time. That makes me so... I don't know. Mad? Sad? Both.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You went back and looked. That took courage — a lot of people can't do that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost didn't. I almost just closed the portfolio app and poured another drink. But I made myself look. And then I just sat there crying in my studio at like two in the morning, which is... a real low point, I'll be honest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two in the morning, crying in your studio, looking at work that reminded you of who you were. And you still didn't close the app.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. I... I kept scrolling. I don't know why. Maybe I was punishing myself. Or maybe I needed to see it. All of it. Years of work and you can kind of see the exact point where things start getting muddier. Technically messier. More chaotic in a way that's not interesting, it's just... sloppy. And I knew, you know? Some part of me knew but I kept telling myself it was evolution.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been protecting a story — that the drinking was feeding the art. And now the evidence is right there in your own work, in your own hands, and that story is getting very hard to hold onto.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. And the thing is, the court thing, the whole reason I'm here — I was so angry about that. I felt like everyone was piling on, like they didn't understand me or my lifestyle or whatever. But now I'm starting to think... maybe this was the thing that finally made me stop and actually look. Which is a really uncomfortable thing to admit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a significant shift from where you were when we started. What do you make of that — the fact that you can see it differently now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'm scared. Like really scared. Because if I take this seriously — if I actually try to change — and the art doesn't come back... then what was any of this for? What did I lose all that time for? That's the part I can't get past. What if sober me is just... boring and bad at painting?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That fear makes complete sense. Let me ask you something — the artist who made that work you saw in your portfolio five or six years ago. Was she boring?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. God, no. She was... she was actually kind of electric. The work had this clarity, this intention. I remember being so proud of some of those pieces. I used to believe in myself in this really quiet, solid way. I haven't felt that in a long time. I forgot I used to feel that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's still in there. The one who worked with clarity and believed in herself quietly. You found her this week when you made yourself look. I want to reflect back what I'm hearing across our time today: you went to the studio, you hit a wall, you reached for the old solution and it didn't work, and instead of stopping there, you went deeper — you looked at your own history honestly, you let yourself grieve what you saw, and you're sitting here right now naming a fear that most people bury. That's not someone who's lost her way. That's someone finding it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I really want to believe that. I think — I think for the first time in a while, I actually do, a little bit. Like just a little. But it's there.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you back, Mike. I know last time wasn't the easiest. How've things been this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... I almost didn't come back, to be honest with you. My wife basically pushed me out the door. I still think my doc is making a way bigger deal out of this than it needs to be. Guys my age, we all got elevated whatever — that's just life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What is it about her concern that bothers you the most?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like — I work hard, man. Forty hours minimum, sometimes more. I'm hauling steel, I'm on my feet all day in the heat. A six-pack at night, that's... I earned that. That's how I decompress. It's not like I'm some guy sitting on a couch drinking vodka at noon. There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking is connected to the work. You put something real into every single day, and that's how you come down from it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. I mean, my dad did the same thing his whole life and he was fine. It's just... it's what you do after a shift like that. But then the doc pulls up these numbers and she's got this look on her face, and I don't know. I didn't sleep great after that appointment.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about that — when she showed you the numbers. What went through your head in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I told her she was overreacting, like I said. But then I got home and I... I looked some of it up. Liver stuff can get serious, right? Like, actually serious. I didn't tell my wife what I found. I just said the doctor was being cautious. Which she was. I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You looked it up, but kept what you found to yourself. That sounds like it's been sitting heavy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I got two kids. Thirteen and sixteen. My daughter's applying to college next year. I'm supposed to walk her down the aisle someday, you know? And I'm sitting there at midnight reading about cirrhosis and I'm thinking — I don't know. This is stupid, forget it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not stupid. That's a father who wants to be there. It took something real to say that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I don't know what I'd even do without it. Like after work, I can't just sit there. My brain doesn't stop. Everything from the day just keeps going and going and the beer is the thing that shuts it off. I don't have another thing that does that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, see if I've got it right. You've been doing hard physical work for a long time, and drinking is genuinely how you've managed to shut your brain down at the end of it. You don't see yourself as someone with a problem — and at the same time, those numbers scared you more than you let on to anyone. And underneath all of it is this picture of your daughter, and wanting to be there for her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...When you say it like that. Yeah. That's pretty much it. I haven't — I don't think I've said any of that out loud before. Not to anybody.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think your daughter would say if she knew you were sitting here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She'd probably cry. She's a sensitive kid. She worries about me, I think. She never says anything but I catch her sometimes — when I crack open a beer after dinner she just... watches me. Doesn't say a word. Just watches.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She sees you. And some part of you has been seeing yourself through her eyes — which is probably why you were on your phone at midnight looking things up instead of just letting it go.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to be the guy who... I don't want her story to be that her dad died young because he was too stubborn to listen to anybody. That's not who I want to be. I think I've known for a while something needed to change. I just — I didn't want to be the one to say it first.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a significant thing to say out loud. Given everything you've shared today — what feels like a possible first step? Something that actually fits your life.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe I start with... not every night. Like, try a few nights without it and see what happens. I'm not saying I'm quitting forever right now, I'm not ready to say that. But maybe start there. See if I can actually do it. See what my brain does.

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know walk-in appointments can feel a little unexpected, so I just want to start by saying there's no agenda here — I'm just curious to hear a little about what brought you in, in your own words.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My mother-in-law basically dragged me here. I mean, not literally, but she's been on my case for weeks and I think she just wanted to feel like she did something. I'm fine, like... I'm dealing with a lot right now, but I don't know why everyone thinks that means I need to be in a — a therapist's office.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it sounds like this wasn't really your idea, and part of you is maybe wondering why you're even here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I have a four-month-old. I'm not sleeping. My body still doesn't feel like mine. And apparently the way I'm coping with all of that is, um, a problem. But like — every new mom has a glass of wine at the end of the night. That's just... that's a thing people do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned coping — what does the end of the night look like for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I put Mia down, and if she actually stays down — which is maybe fifty percent of the time — I just... I pour a glass of wine. Or two. And I sit on the couch and I don't talk to anyone and I don't have to be needed by anyone for like forty-five minutes. And that's it. That's my whole thing. I'm not, like, falling down drunk, I'm not neglecting her, I'm not — I don't know what everyone wants from me. What am I supposed to do, just cry into a pillow?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a tremendous amount right now — the exhaustion, the pressure of being needed constantly, and then feeling judged on top of it all. That forty-five minutes sounds like the only space that's actually yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's exactly it. Nobody gets that. My husband tries, he really does, but he went back to work and I'm just... I'm home with her all day and then I'm supposed to also be, like, present and cheerful and — yeah. The wine is the only thing that turns my brain off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say it turns your brain off — what's your brain doing when it's on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... running. All the time. Like, is she gaining enough weight, did I do tummy time long enough, am I bonding with her the right way, is she going to be okay... and then underneath all of that there's this other thing, this voice that's like — are you okay? And I don't really want to look at that one. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a voice asking if you're okay, and it feels easier to not look at it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because if I look at it... I don't know. I'm scared of what I'll find, I think. Like what if I look and the answer is no, I'm not okay, and then what? I still have to get up tomorrow and take care of her. I can't just fall apart. She needs me to not fall apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like Mia is really at the center of this for you. When you imagine what you want things to look like — for her, for you — what comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to be... present. Like, actually present. Not just physically there while my brain is somewhere else. I want to be the mom who remembers things, who's not just getting through the day until I can pour that glass. I didn't think I'd be thinking about wine at two in the afternoon, you know? That part... that part worries me a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think there's something important here. You came in today not by choice, feeling like nothing was really wrong. And as we've been talking, you've shared that you're exhausted and overwhelmed, that there's a voice inside asking if you're okay that you've been afraid to look at, and that part of you is already noticing the wine has started to take up more space than you want it to. And underneath all of that — what you actually want — is to be genuinely present for Mia.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. When you say it like that... I mean. Yeah. That's — that's pretty much it. I didn't come in here thinking I'd say any of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you saying that. What feels like the most important thing to you, coming out of today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I need to actually answer that question. The 'are you okay' one. Not for my mother-in-law or whoever. But because Mia's going to remember things eventually, you know? She's going to remember what her mom was like. And I want — I want her to have a mom who was actually there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage to say — and to sit with. The fact that you're already thinking about what Mia will carry with her, that's not someone who doesn't care. That's someone who cares deeply. Whatever comes next, I think that love is a pretty solid place to start from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I haven't cried yet this whole conversation. Which is impressive because I cry at, like, paper towel commercials now. But yeah. I think I want to come back. If that's — if that's something I can do.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know this might feel a bit strange — sitting across from someone you've never met, talking about personal stuff. I won't pretend otherwise. So let me just start simple: what's on your mind walking in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I feel like I got... maneuvered into this. My wife basically said it was either I come here or — well, she was pretty clear about the alternative. So. Here I am. I'm not trying to be rude about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because you care about the marriage — even if you're not fully convinced you need to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, sure. Yeah. I care about the marriage, of course I do. But do I think I have some big drinking problem? No. I think she overreacts sometimes. And then my doctor piled on last month with his little... speech. So now everyone's got an opinion all of a sudden.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you've been hearing this from a few different directions lately. I'm curious — when you're having a drink in the evening, what does that look like? What's that time of day actually like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... winding down. Watching the news, maybe some baseball. A few beers, sometimes a scotch. It's nothing dramatic. I'm not stumbling around, I'm not driving anywhere, I'm not hurting anybody. It's just quiet. Everything is very quiet now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Everything is very quiet now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't mean it like — look, I know how that sounds. But I worked forty-two years. I had a team, I had meetings, I had things to do. People needed me for things. And now it's just... nothing. My wife's got her book clubs, her friends, her whatever. And I'm sitting there like furniture. So yeah, I have a drink. Sue me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There was a whole world built around who you were at work. And then that just... stopped.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And nobody — nobody tells you that's going to happen. You think retirement is going to be this great thing and then you get there and... I don't know what I'm doing half the time. It's embarrassing to even say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to admit that — that you feel lost. Walk me through what a typical day actually looks like for you right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. I wake up. Coffee. Read the news online. Maybe go for a walk if it's not too cold. Sandra goes out, does her thing. I cook sometimes, I guess. And then... yeah, by four or five o'clock I'm having a drink. And I keep thinking I should be doing something else but I don't — I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've recognized something that a lot of people take a long time to see — that the drinking is filling a space that used to be filled by something else. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor said my liver enzymes are elevated. I had to look that up when I got home. Not at crisis level, he said, but... not good either. And then Sandra found my search history and it scared her. Scared me too, honestly. I don't want to get sick. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you imagine yourself five years from now — what does life look like if things stay as they are? And what does it look like if something shifts?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: If nothing changes... maybe Sandra leaves. Health gets worse. I don't — I don't want to be one of those guys. I've seen it. My father drank. Not violent or anything, he just kind of... disappeared into it. And I used to look at him and think, 'That's not going to be me.' And here I am talking to you. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I've got this right. You built an identity around your work for over forty years, and retirement took that away faster than you expected. The drinking started as a way to manage the quiet — the loneliness, the loss of purpose. Now the people you love are worried, your body's sending signals, and somewhere in all of this you're thinking about your father, and about who you want to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. Yeah, that's pretty much it. When you put it like that it sounds... I don't know if I'm ready to quit entirely, that feels like a lot. But I think — I think I need to figure out what I'm doing with myself. Because the drinking, that's just the symptom, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today feeling like you were pushed. And somewhere in this conversation you started asking your own questions. What feels like a realistic first step — something that actually fits your life right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... talking to Sandra. Really talking, not just nodding. I've been shutting her out because I didn't want to admit I was struggling. And maybe looking into some kind of — I don't know — activity, group, something. I can't just keep sitting in that house. I'm 65, not 95. I've still got time. I hope I've got time.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's really good to see you again. I know this week was a hard one... how are you doing today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I almost didn't come. I sat in my car for like twenty minutes thinking about just driving home. I don't... I don't even know what I'm supposed to get out of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You almost didn't come... and yet here you are. Something brought you through that door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well I had a terrible week, didn't I. Three nights in a row I just — yeah. And then my daughter called and she could tell, and we had this awful argument and she started crying and I just... Fine. I'm here. But I'm not — I am not saying I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a really painful few days. The argument with your daughter on top of everything else...

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She doesn't understand. Nobody does. They all think I should just be over it by now. Eight months. Like there's some kind of deadline on missing your husband of thirty years. Thirty years. And everyone just expects you to carry on like nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thirty years together... and the world just expects you to keep going. That is an enormous amount of loss to be carrying, especially alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I found his reading glasses. That's — that's what set me off this week. They were in the pocket of his old coat and I just... I don't know. It's stupid. It's just a pair of glasses.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not stupid at all. Those small things... they hold so much of a person.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I know the drinking isn't — I mean, I know it's not... look, I'm not an idiot. It's just that when I have a couple glasses it gets quieter. *laughs softly* In my head, I mean. Everything just settles down for a little while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gives you some relief from all that noise inside.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. But then... you wake up at three in the morning and it's all just sitting right there waiting for you. And the house is so — God, it is so quiet. Not a good quiet. Just... empty. I keep thinking I hear him in the other room.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two different kinds of quiet. The one the wine gives you, and then the one that comes after at three in the morning — and that second one is so much harder to be in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: We used to watch the news together every night. Even when we didn't talk. We'd just... sit there. And that was enough, you know? I didn't need anything else. Now I turn the TV on and I just — I can't stand the sound of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Just being there together, without needing to say anything — that mattered so deeply to you. That kind of companionship.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I don't want to lose myself on top of losing him. I think that's what scares me, if I'm being honest. That I'm turning into someone he wouldn't even recognize. Someone I don't recognize.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today not even sure why you were here. And in the middle of all this pain, you just said something really significant — that there's a part of you that is still fighting to hold onto who you are. That part of you came through that door today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... *long pause* He would have hated seeing me like this. But he also would have just... sat next to me and not said anything and that would have been enough. *voice breaks* I miss him so much. I just miss him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let yourself feel that for a moment... *pause* When you picture the woman he knew — the one he would have sat beside — what do you think she needs most right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone to talk to, I think. Not... not wine. Someone real. I've been pushing everyone away because it hurts less than needing them and having them not know what to say. But maybe... maybe I should call my daughter back. Actually call her, not just text.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. After everything that happened... that took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't have a choice. Judge said show up or go back to holding. So. Here I am. Don't read too much into it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here under pressure and you're pissed off about it. I get that. Can you tell me what happened — what landed you in the ER?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Does it even matter? Whatever I say ends up in a file and then the DA uses it against me. That's how this whole thing works. You're not here to help me, you're here to document me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been through this system before and it hasn't felt safe. You've been used against yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... look. I drank, okay? Too much. I fell, hit my head on the counter, needed stitches. There. Done. Can we check the box and move on?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were alone when it happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter was... she was in the next room. She's eight. She — she's the one who called 911. Eight years old calling 911 because her dad is on the kitchen floor. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text:
...
She heard all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She wasn't supposed to be awake. I thought — I don't know what I thought. I thought I had it under control, I always think that, and then... I don't know. I woke up with paramedics over me and she was just standing there in her pajamas.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't want her to see that. That's clear. That you're sitting here carrying that — that tells me something about who you are as her father.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not a bad dad. I'm not. I love my kid more than anything. I just... I don't know how to — it's like the second I'm alone the whole thing just, um. Collapses.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture her standing there in those pajamas — what do you think that night is going to mean for her? Not just right now, but... down the road?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. When the paramedics were putting me on the stretcher she kept saying 'daddy wake up, daddy wake up' and I could hear her, I just couldn't — I couldn't answer her. And I keep thinking about that. What does a kid do with that? What does that... what does that make me in her head?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I can hold all of this for a second. You came today not because you wanted to — and you're still angry about that, that's real. But something happened this week that cracked something open. Your daughter called 911. She stood in the dark in her pajamas and she was terrified. And even as part of you is still fighting this whole situation... there's another part of you that can't stop hearing her voice.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
When you say it like that...
[long pause]
I keep telling myself I'm not that guy. I'm not my father, I'm not — but last night I was exactly that guy. On the floor. His kid scared.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just brought up your father. Who do you want to be for her — when she's grown and she looks back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone she doesn't have to worry about. Someone steady. My dad was... it doesn't matter, he's gone. But I grew up scared all the time, like, just waiting for the next thing. And I swore I'd never — I swore she would never feel that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know exactly what that fear feels like from the inside. You lived it. And you came in here today — stitches in your head, court breathing down your neck, every reason to shut down — and you said that out loud. That's not nothing. That's the beginning of something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
I never thought about it that way. Like I'm spending all this energy trying not to become him and maybe I... maybe I already am. A little.
[quiet]
Maybe I actually need to do something different. Like really different. Not just... show up and check the box.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for showing up today, Marcus. I know this probably wasn't your idea, so... I just want you to know there's no agenda here. I'm just curious about you and what's going on in your life. What would you say brought you in today, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My buddy Ray basically ambushed me. Him and my wife cooked something up and... look, I'm only here because Ray served with me and I owe him that much. I don't — I'm not someone who needs to sit and talk about his feelings, if that's what this is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here out of loyalty to Ray. That says something real about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... Ray's been through it. We both have. And I don't know, people act like having a few drinks after what we've seen is some kind of — it's not a disorder. It's just... that's how you decompress. That's how it worked over there, that's how it works when you get back. Everybody drank. It's not like I'm some kind of... I'm not sitting in a ditch somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's been part of the culture for a long time — a way of getting through things that most people can't even imagine. And you've carried a lot, Marcus. I'm not here to argue with any of that. I guess I'm just wondering... when you picture your life, like five years from now, what does it look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I don't know. I haven't really — that's a weird question. Um. I guess I figured things would just kind of... settle down. Like eventually it gets easier and you find your footing and... I don't know. I thought Diane and me would be good by now. I thought I'd be good by now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Diane is your wife. It sounds like things between you two are... not where you hoped they'd be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said she's done. Like, those words — 'I'm done.' She didn't say divorce exactly but she... she packed a bag two weeks ago and went to her sister's. She came back but it's — it's bad. And I get it, like, I know I haven't been... easy to be around. But she knew who she married. She knew what the Army was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She came back. Even after packing that bag, she came back. What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I think she's still holding on to something. To who I used to be, maybe. And I — that kills me more than if she had just stayed gone, honestly. Because it means she still... she hasn't given up on me completely. And I don't know if I deserve that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's still holding on. And part of you... part of you wants to be worth holding on to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I do. I just — I don't know how to be that guy anymore. The drinking... okay, look. I'm not saying it's nothing. I'm saying it's the only thing that turns the volume down. You know? It gets quiet when I drink. And I know that sounds... I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like a character flaw to me. It sounds like someone who found the only tool he had to manage something overwhelming — and that tool came with a cost he didn't fully see coming. Can I ask, before the drinking got heavier, what did you used to do to wind down?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I used to run. Like, a lot. Six, seven miles sometimes before breakfast. And I'd... Diane and I used to cook together on Sundays. Stupid stuff like that. I haven't — I don't run anymore. My knee's messed up but also I just... I don't have that in me right now. I wake up and I'm already exhausted.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sunday cooking with Diane. Running in the early morning. Those weren't small things — that was you, taking care of yourself, connecting with the person you love. That version of you isn't gone, Marcus. He's just buried under a lot of weight right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I haven't thought about the Sunday cooking in a while. She would put on that — she has this terrible playlist. Like, old R&B she's had since college. I used to make fun of her for it. I would give anything to hear that playlist right now, man. I'm serious.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — and I'm not trying to put words in your mouth — but it sounds like there's a part of you that's actually been wanting something different for a while now. What would it mean to you, if you could find a way to get some of that back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... I don't know, man. Like I could breathe again? Like maybe I didn't come home from that place and just — ruin everything I actually cared about. Maybe there's still time to not be the guy who loses his family because he couldn't figure out how to come back from a war. I don't want to be that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Marcus, I want to reflect something back to you, because I think it matters. You came in today saying you didn't need this, that you were only here for Ray. But somewhere in the last twenty minutes, you told me about Diane coming back, about Sunday mornings, about not wanting to lose the people you love. That's not a man who's given up. That's a man who still has a lot to fight for. I think you know what direction you want to go. And I'd really like to help you figure out the path, if you're open to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, okay. I'm... I'm open to it. I'm not saying I have it all figured out or that this is gonna be easy but... yeah. Let's — I'll try. I can try.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Dr. Reyes mentioned things got pretty rough this week. I'm glad you came back. What's it like being here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Same as last time. Pointless. My parents basically dragged me here so, whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Pointless.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah like... what's talking about it gonna do? Nothing changes. I come here, you write stuff down, I go home, my parents are still on my case. It's like a waste of everyone's time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you. Before we go any further — tell me what happened this week. From your point of view.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They found bottles again. Under my bed this time. My dad completely lost it, my mom was... I don't know. They think I'm like, some alcoholic or something. I'm sixteen. I had a few beers. It's not that deep.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're standing, the bigger problem isn't the drinking — it's everyone overreacting to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. My dad has a beer every single night, sometimes more, and nobody's hauling him in here. But I do it and suddenly I'm the problem? That's — yeah. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That does sound unfair. I want to ask you something, and you don't have to answer if it doesn't feel right — what's usually going on right before you go for the beers?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Why does everyone keep asking me that? I just — look. I had a rough week, I drank, it happened. Can you just like sign whatever form they need so I can leave? I don't want to talk about why.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're angry. And underneath that, it sounds like you're exhausted from everyone picking at something you feel like they don't actually understand.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... yeah. Like I'm under a microscope. Everything at home is — I don't know. It's loud. Like all the time it's loud and I'm just... I'm the bad guy now. Every single thing is suddenly my fault.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying something really heavy. That's real, and it makes sense that it wears on you. When you said it's loud at home — what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... um. My parents fight a lot. Not like hitting or whatever, just — yelling, slamming doors. And then they found the bottles and my mom just... she was crying. Not yelling. Just standing there crying and looking at me and I didn't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — your mom not yelling, just crying — that landed differently than the anger did.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean I knew they'd be pissed, I was ready for that. But she just looked so... I don't know. Tired. Like I did that. And I just needed it to stop for a little while, y'know? The noise in my head. I didn't mean for her to look like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, tell me if I'm getting it wrong. There's a lot of noise at home — fighting, tension — and it gets overwhelming. The drinking quiets that down for a bit. But then your mom's face, and that's sitting with you now in a different way. You didn't want to hurt her. You were just trying to get some relief.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I'm not trying to like, blow up my life. I'm not stupid. I just — I don't know what else to do when it gets like that. My brain just won't stop and drinking is the only thing that actually works. Or, I mean... worked. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you if you could find a way to make it quieter — without it costing you what it's been costing you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... things wouldn't be so messed up, I guess. My mom wouldn't look at me like that. Maybe I'd actually sleep. I don't know if I know how to do that, like I don't even know where to start, but... maybe that's worth figuring out. Maybe.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this might not be where you'd choose to spend your Thursday afternoon. There's no agenda here, no pressure. I'd just like to hear from you — what brought you in, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My friends basically made me come. They got all worried after my physical and thought I needed to, like, talk to someone. I don't... I mean, I don't really see the point, honestly. I've done this before and it never — it never actually does anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here more for them than for yourself right now. And you've been through something like this before... and it didn't really land.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I mean, I love my friends, I do, but they kind of blew everything way out of proportion. One bad lab result and suddenly I'm like... an alcoholic or something. I'm in college. Everyone drinks. Like, that's just what you do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me a little more about that — when you actually got those results, what was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... honestly? It sucked. The doctor was kind of freaking out about my liver enzymes or whatever, and I just... I don't know. It doesn't even matter. Even if I tried to cut back — I've tried before. Nothing ever sticks. I can't change, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about hearing that from the doctor hit differently... and at the same time there's this really heavy feeling underneath it — like you've already tried, it hasn't worked, so why bother going through it again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I saw two other counselors before you. One just kept asking me how I felt over and over. The other one gave me worksheets. Like — actual printed worksheets. Cool, thanks, that totally fixed everything. It doesn't work. I don't work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet here you are. You walked through that door today even after all of that. That's... that's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I showed up because my roommate literally drove me here and wouldn't leave until I went inside. That's not me wanting to be here. Don't, like... don't read too much into it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. I won't. ... Do you remember what the doctor actually said to you — like, specifically?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said my liver enzymes were elevated. And something about blood pressure. She asked how much I drink and I told her and she just... kind of stared at me for a second. Like I was already broken or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That look she gave you — what did that bring up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. My uncle, he, um... he had drinking problems. Like real ones. And he got really sick when he was like forty-something. And I remember thinking when I was a kid, I'm never gonna be like that. And then she looked at me that way and I just... I don't want to think about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image of your uncle... it's been sitting somewhere in the back of your mind this whole time. Even when you didn't want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Maybe. I'm not him — I'm twenty-one, not forty-something. But I guess... I don't know, maybe I've kind of been trying not to think about it on purpose. Which sounds stupid when I actually say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. ... When you picture yourself at thirty — what does that look like? What do you want it to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to have my stuff together. Like, a real job, not be a mess. I don't want to still be doing... this. I don't want to be that guy. I just never really thought about it being connected, you know? Like what I do now actually mattering for later.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this version of you at thirty — things together, not walking the same road your uncle did. And today, when that doctor looked at you that way, something in you heard a warning you've been working hard to tune out. You're not convinced anything can actually change, and you didn't exactly choose to be here... but some part of you is thinking about it. That part showed up today too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess. I'm not saying I'm ready to, like, do anything about it. But... yeah. Maybe I'm thinking about it a little.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. You look like you've had a rough week — want to tell me about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't really want to be here, if I'm being honest. Judge says I have to come so here I am. That's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because you have to be, and that doesn't sit right with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Wouldn't sit right with you either. I made one mistake and now I'm being treated like I'm some kind of — I don't know, like I'm a bad person or something. My kids need me at home. I don't have time to sit in an office every week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what happened this week.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay, yeah, it was bad. Marcus had a meltdown at school, I got a call from his teacher right in the middle of a work deadline, and I just — look, I had more than a couple glasses of wine that night. I know how that sounds. But what was I supposed to do? There's nobody else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Everything collapsed at once — work, Marcus, no one to hand it off to. And you've been carrying that weight alone for a long time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It is a lot. And I'm not making excuses, I'm just — it's always just me, you know? And I was actually doing okay for a stretch before this. Like genuinely okay. And then this week just... it fell apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were doing okay for a stretch — that's worth paying attention to. Something in you knows how to pull back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I went four days without opening a bottle. Which — for where I've been lately, that's actually kind of a thing for me. I didn't think it counted for much but... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four days is real. What was different about those four days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... Sofia. She's nine and she asked me once why I keep falling asleep on the couch. And I just — I made this kind of promise to myself that I wasn't going to be that person for her anymore. And for those four days I kept it. I actually kept it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sofia's watching, and that matters to you more than almost anything else. Keeping that quiet promise — even for four days — that's you being the mother you want to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And then I just blew it again. And I... I hate that. I hate that she might have seen me. I don't know if she did but she could've and that — that's the part that actually keeps me up at night. Not the court stuff. That.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you could change one thing about what Sofia grows up thinking is normal — what would it be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want her to think that when things get hard you just... check out. Because that's what my mom did. I know what it feels like to be on the other side of that and I swore — I swore I wasn't going to be that. I made that promise to myself a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know exactly what it's like to be Sofia right now. That knowing — that's not something everyone has. That's actually a powerful reason to do this differently.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never... said it out loud like that before. That she might be sitting with what I sat with. God. That hits different when you say it that way. I don't want that for her. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just hold up what I've been hearing today. You came in frustrated, feeling like you had no choice but to be here. And somewhere along the way you started talking about Sofia, about four days of keeping a promise to yourself, about not wanting to pass something painful down to your daughter — something you know from the inside. That's not nothing. That's actually everything. What do you want to do with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know exactly what it looks like yet. But I think I want to actually try. Not just white-knuckle it for a few days and then fall apart. Something has to actually change. I just — I don't know how. But I want to figure it out. I think I'm ready to try to figure it out.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you made it in today. That took something, coming here — especially after yesterday. There's no agenda, no rush. We can just... sit here for a minute if you need to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Um. I don't really — I'm not sure why I'm here, honestly. The doctor said I should talk to someone, so... here I am. I'm fine, though. Like, it was just a long week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A long week. ... What's been making it long?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... everything? I've got two kids, I work full time, there's no — there's nobody else helping. My youngest had a fever last week on top of everything. It's just a lot. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No one else. You're carrying all of this by yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I know people have it worse, I know that. It's not like I'm — I'm not complaining. It's just sometimes at the end of the day I need to turn my brain off for a little bit, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does that look like for you — turning your brain off at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... wine, mostly. Like a glass of wine when the kids are in bed, just to decompress. It's — everyone does that, right? I see it on every Instagram mom page. 'Wine o'clock.' It's not like I'm doing anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like that glass of wine is... the only moment that belongs to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — huh. I never thought of it like that but yeah. It's like the only quiet I get. And I know I've been having more than one lately, I'll be honest about that. It's just... the last couple months have been really rough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're being really honest with yourself right now. That's not easy — especially sitting here for the first time, especially after yesterday.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I keep thinking about my girls. I'm — I'm terrified of becoming my mom, you know? She drank. It was bad. And I swore I'd never be that. And now I'm sitting in this office and I... ... Sorry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Don't apologize. ... That fear — becoming your mom — that lives somewhere really deep in you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never talk about that. Just — yeah. My girls are eight and eleven. And the other night my oldest, she asked me why I always have my 'special juice.' And I laughed it off but inside I was like... oh god. Oh god.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She noticed. ... And you noticed her noticing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I think that's why I ended up in the ER honestly. Not just because of the physical stuff — that scared me too. But I think... some part of me needed someone to stop me. Or at least just... look at me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I just take a moment and reflect back what I'm hearing? You came in here after a night that scared you — physically and in a deeper way. You're exhausted, you're alone, and that wine became the one thing that was yours, the only way to breathe. And underneath all of that is this fear — about your mom, about your girls, about who you might be becoming. And some part of you reached out. That part brought you here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that I just... *exhales* ...I don't want to be that person. I love my kids so much. I just got so tired. And I didn't know what else to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You found your way here — even when you were scared, even when part of you was saying you were fine. That matters. What would it mean to you to start figuring out what else there could be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know yet. But... I think I want to find out. Like maybe — maybe this is where I start. I don't know. But yeah. I think I'm ready to at least try.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today, even with everything on your plate. I know you mentioned you're between classes, so I want to make sure we use this time in a way that actually feels worth it for you. What's been weighing on you most lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My boss. Like, my company basically made me come here — well, not here specifically, but... therapy. Which, no offense, feels a little ridiculous for what happened. It was one night. One. And now suddenly I'm doing mandatory counseling and everyone's looking at me like I'm — I don't know, like I have a drinking problem or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it feels like a lot of people have drawn really big conclusions from one night, and that doesn't sit right with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. Like, I work incredibly hard — I'm in marketing, the culture is... it's just how things work, you know? Happy hours, client dinners, team events. Everyone drinks. It's not like I showed up to work drunk or whatever. I was driving home from a work event and I just... misjudged. It happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something real in your career — that matters, and it sounds like you take it seriously. I'm curious... when you say you misjudged that night, what does that actually mean for you? What was going on inside?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I had more than I usually do, I guess. It was a stressful week and the client dinner just kept going and I didn't want to be the person who leaves early, you know? And then I just — I didn't think I was that bad. I felt fine. But apparently I wasn't. And now I have a DUI on my record and I could lose my license and... yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm embarrassed, okay? Is that what you want to hear? I'm really embarrassed. My parents found out and my mom cried, which was — that was awful. And I keep thinking like, what if it had been worse? What if someone had been in the road, or... I don't let myself go there very much because it's just too — it's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — what could have happened — it visits you even when you try to push it away. There's a part of you that already understands the weight of that night, even if another part is still fighting to make it smaller.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think that's... yeah. I don't know. I keep going back and forth between like, 'this is so overblown' and then three in the morning I'm spiraling about it. I can't really sleep. I've been drinking a bit more actually, which I know sounds — I know how that sounds, but it helps me turn my brain off at night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something that took some courage — noticing that you've been drinking more to quiet the noise. That self-awareness matters. I want to ask you something, and take your time with it: when you imagine your life two years from now, the version of you that feels good about who she is... what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Um... I don't know. I mean, I want to make director level at my company by thirty, that's always been the goal. And I want... I want to not feel like I'm white-knuckling it through every week, I guess. Like, I'm so tired. I'm really, really tired and I don't think I've said that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Really tired. And underneath all the ambition and the work events and holding it together for everyone else... there's someone who is exhausted and maybe hasn't had a chance to just stop.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't really know how to stop. That's the thing. Like, slowing down feels dangerous? Which sounds insane when I say it. But if I stop moving I think I might actually feel how bad things have gotten and that's... I don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound insane at all. It sounds like you've been protecting yourself the best way you knew how. And the drinking — keeping things numb, keeping things moving — it's been doing a job for you. Even if the cost is getting higher.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The cost is really high. Like, a DUI is not... that's not who I thought I was. I grew up watching my uncle lose everything to drinking and I swore I was different. And maybe I am different, maybe this really is just stress and bad timing, but... I don't know. I honestly don't know anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something really significant just happened — you brought up your uncle. You've carried that fear a long time, the fear of becoming something you swore you wouldn't. What would it mean for you to take this moment seriously, not because your employer said to, but because you said to?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... it would mean I actually care about myself. Which sounds like a therapy cliche but I think I actually haven't been doing that. I've been caring about my performance review and what my boss thinks and whether I'm likable enough at networking events and — God, when did I stop mattering to myself? That's a really depressing question.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today feeling pushed and frustrated, ready to check a box. And somewhere in the last forty minutes, you found something real — the exhaustion, the fear, the part of you that knows this matters. That took guts. I want you to hold onto that question you just asked yourself, because I think you already know the answer. Can we talk about what a next step might look like — one that's yours, not your employer's?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think I want to come back. And I think I need to actually be honest with myself about how much I'm drinking, not just like — not just defend it. I don't know what that looks like yet but... I want to figure it out. I actually want to.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's really good to see you again. I know last time felt a little... intense, maybe, and I just want you to know there's no agenda today — we go wherever feels right to you. So how have things been since we last talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, I mean — fine? Like, honestly it's been a crazy week. I had two brand deals close and then a whole collab trip to Miami, so... yeah. Good. I'm good. I don't even know why I feel nervous right now, that's so weird, I'm not usually like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The nervousness surprised you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha — yeah, I guess. It's just... this whole setup feels very clinical, you know? Like, I'm not some... person with a problem. I'm just me. And apparently my doctor has decided that me is a problem, which, honestly? Rude.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It can feel really strange to be here when you don't see yourself that way. I'm curious — you came back today. What made you decide to come back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I said I would? I'm not someone who backs out of things. Like, I committed, so I'm here. And also — okay, I don't know, I think part of me was just like... why is everyone suddenly so worried? My friends, my doctor, now you. It's a lot of people to suddenly be like, hey, Sienna, we have concerns. That's... it's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this chorus of concern around you, and it's started to feel like pressure coming from all sides.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Because like — my followers love seeing me out, my whole brand is built on that energy. And my friend group, we've been going out together since college, that's just what we do. No one is sitting at home on a Saturday night. That's just... life. That's just how people socialize.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's woven into so much — your career, your friendships, your whole identity almost. What do you think it would mean for all of that, if things did start to look different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I — okay, see, this is where I get stressed. Because what does that even look like? Like, I stop going out and I post about... green smoothies? My audience would disappear overnight. My friends would think something was seriously wrong with me. It's not as simple as just 'drink less,' it's like — it touches everything. It's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see really clearly how much is attached to it. And you're also someone who showed up here, twice, even when part of you really didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I'm not someone who just sticks her head in the sand, I guess. Like, I take care of myself. I work out, I eat well, I get my check-ups. I'm responsible. I just... also like to have fun. Those aren't mutually exclusive.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Someone who pays attention to herself, who doesn't look away from things. And I noticed — just now, there was this small hesitation before you finished that sentence. What was in that pause?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I don't know. I think sometimes I wonder if the fun is still actually fun, or if it's just like... automatic? Like I don't even decide anymore, I just — Thursday comes, someone texts the group chat, and I go. But I'm sure that's normal. Everyone's on autopilot sometimes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something that used to feel like a choice has started to feel more like something you just... do, without really deciding. What's it like to sit with that thought?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Heavy, I think. Like it's not — it's not a comfortable thought, honestly. I'd rather not think about it. But it's been there. Kind of in the back of my head for a while now and I just keep pushing it down.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That thought keeps coming back, even when you'd prefer it stayed quiet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Which is so annoying. Because my life is good. Like, objectively — I have a career I built from nothing, I have friends, I travel, I have no reason to be sitting in this office. But I'm here. And last weekend I noticed I already had a headache before we even went out, because I was anxious about... keeping up, I think. Which I've never noticed before. Or maybe I just never let myself notice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back today. You've been carrying this quiet, uncomfortable question even while everything looks great from the outside. And now there's this headache — your body sending a signal before the night even started. You notice things, Sienna. Even the things you'd rather not.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't really know what to do with that. But yeah. I guess I am. Noticing.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today, George. I know it's your first day out of detox, and that's... that's not a small thing. How are you feeling right now, sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Tired, mostly. Just... tired. My hands were still shaking this morning, not as bad as last week, but. I don't know. I made it through, I guess. That's something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You made it through. And you showed up today. What's been going through your mind this past week, while you were in there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Shame, mostly. About the thing at work — I was only doing two days a week at the hardware store, just to have something to do, you know, and I showed up... not right. And my daughter found out. She barely looks at me now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a heavy thing to carry — the shame about what happened, and then feeling your daughter pull back. What does a regular day actually look like for you now, since you retired?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Empty. I wake up and... there's nothing. My wife passed four years ago. The kids have their own lives. I had a routine — the job, the structure — and then retirement hit and it just... disappeared. I'd sit with the TV on, not even knowing what I was watching, and somehow it'd be five o'clock and I'd already had a few.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The days just dissolve. No shape to them. And the drinking sort of filled that space.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It did. And I knew — the doctor told me about my liver last spring, I'm not an idiot — but it just didn't... it didn't feel like it mattered that much. What was I protecting myself for? To sit alone in that house?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real question — what are you protecting yourself for. I want to ask you something directly. Is there anything, or anyone, that felt worth sticking around for? Even a little. It doesn't have to be big.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My granddaughter. She's seven. She still calls me Grandpa like I'm... like I'm someone worth calling. I haven't seen her much lately. I don't want her to — um — I don't want her to know me like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
