utterances.text: She calls you like you're someone worth calling. That's not nothing, George. You're sitting here the day after detox, and the first thing that comes to mind when I ask what matters — it's her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I don't know when I stopped being someone she could be proud of. Part of me thinks it's already too late anyway, the liver stuff, the drinking — but then I think about her and I... I don't know. It's like two different voices.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two voices. One saying it's too late, one thinking about her. What is the voice thinking about her actually saying?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think it's saying... I want more time. Good time. Not just existing. I worked hard my whole life. I was a decent father, I think. Retirement just — it hit me like a wall and I didn't know how to be a person without all that. Without the job, without Margaret.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You built a life with structure and purpose — work, family, being a provider. When that ended, the bottom dropped out. And the drinking was never really about alcohol. It was about not knowing how to be George anymore. And now, on the other side of detox, there's still a part of you that wants to find that — for yourself, and for her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's exactly it. Nobody's said it like that before. I'm not — I mean, I know I was drinking too much, clearly — but that's not who I am. I just got lost. And I'm sixty-five and I'm thinking, do I have enough time to get unlost?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've already started. You went through a week of detox. You're sitting in this chair. And the fact that you're asking 'do I have enough time' — that's not a hopeless question. That's a man who still wants something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do. I think I do. I want to — maybe volunteer somewhere, find something to do with my mornings. And I need to call my daughter. Actually call her, not just think about calling her. I've been hiding from everyone. That has to stop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like someone who knows what he needs. If you were going to take one step this week — just one — what feels most real to you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Call my daughter. Tonight. No rehearsing, no waiting until I feel ready — I just do it. Tell her I'm sorry and I'm trying. That's where I start.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey... I'm really glad you were able to join today. I know this probably wasn't your idea. Before we get into anything, I just want you to know — nothing you say here goes back to your school or your family unless I'm worried you're in real danger. This is just... yours. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, whatever. I mean, sure. I still don't get why I have to be here. Like, it was one party. Literally everyone drinks. Everyone. And I'm the one sitting here doing... this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like you got singled out. Like... why you, when everyone else was doing the exact same thing and they're just going about their week.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. My friends aren't in therapy right now. They're at school, hanging out, whatever — and I'm here because my mom freaked out and the school made a whole thing out of it. It's so unfair. Like, nobody cares when other kids do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That distance — being the one here while your friends are just... living their lives. What does it feel like, sitting with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It feels like I'm being treated like a criminal when I literally just had a couple drinks at a party. My mom is acting like I'm some kind of — I don't know. Like, I made one mistake and now I'm suddenly a problem. I'm not a problem. I'm a normal person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You weren't trying to hurt anyone. You were just... being a teenager, doing what everyone around you was doing. And now here you are, having to explain yourself for it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [pause] I mean... okay. Fine. I probably shouldn't have been drinking at a school thing. That was kind of dumb, I know how schools are. But that's, like, a different thing. That doesn't mean I have a problem with drinking. Why does everyone jump straight to that?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It took something to say that — 'that was kind of dumb.' A lot of people wouldn't. [pause] I hear you though. You're not saying drinking is the problem. You're saying being you, in that moment, with those people... that felt normal.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like, my friends were all doing it and I just... I didn't want to be the weird one standing there with a water bottle. That sounds stupid when I say it out loud but like... you know how it is. Or maybe you don't. [shrugs]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. Wanting to belong, not wanting to be the one standing apart from everybody else — that's one of the most human things there is. [pause] That matters to you. These people matter to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They're like... they're the only people I actually feel like myself around, you know? [quieter] At home it's always — are you studying, what are you doing next year, do you have a plan — and with my friends I can just exist. The drinking is kind of just... it's just background. It's social.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's tied to something that really matters — those friendships, that feeling of being able to just breathe. [long pause] When you say you feel like yourself with them... what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... I don't have to have everything figured out. I don't have to be perfect or whatever. [pause] I guess... I don't know. It's the only place that doesn't feel like pressure. Like constant pressure. [quieter] The drinking is just kind of... it's just there. It's what happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking is just there. But underneath it — what you're really describing is this place where you finally get to put everything down. All the pressure, all the expectations. Just... exhale.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [pause] Yeah, that's... that's kind of exactly it. [small silence] I never really thought about it like that. Like, maybe it's not even really about the drinking. Maybe it's just... I need somewhere that isn't — I don't know. Everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in here not wanting to be here, pretty sure this was a waste of time — and in the last few minutes you just named something really important. That the drinking isn't the whole story. That what you're actually reaching for is somewhere safe to land. Somewhere that isn't all expectations and unanswered questions. [pause] That took a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [quiet laugh, then more serious] I mean... when you say it like that. [pause] I do get kind of scared sometimes. Like... what if I'm using it to not think? About college, or my parents fighting all the time, or just — I don't know. Everything feels really big right now and it's easier when I don't have to feel it all. [trails off]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That right there — what you just said — that took real courage. [pause] So I want to ask you something, and there's genuinely no right answer. Not what your mom wants, not what your school is expecting. What does you want for yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I want to feel okay without needing it. Like, be able to go somewhere and just — be there, without it being a thing. [pause] I don't know if that's even possible for me right now but... yeah. That's what I actually want. I think.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I know this week was harder than the last few — I'm glad you're here. How are you sitting with everything right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I'm here, aren't I? Look, I don't — I'm not sure "rough patch" is even the right word. Things got complicated at work. Q2 projections are a mess, I had three board calls in four days, and my wife decides now is the time to make everything about my drinking. So. Yeah. I'm great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're carrying a lot right now — the pressure at work is real, and then you come home and instead of... quiet, there's another confrontation waiting for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. That's exactly it. I've been running this company for eleven years. Eleven years. I've managed crises that would put most people in a hospital, and I handle it. I always handle it. So she points at the scotch like it's the problem, and I'm supposed to — what, apologize? For having a drink after a sixteen-hour day?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What did that look like — the moment she brought it up this week? Walk me through it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... Wednesday night. I'd just gotten off a call at like 10:30, and I poured myself a drink, and she was sitting at the kitchen table and she just — she had this look. And she said something like, "again." Just that one word. And I don't know, I just... I didn't have anything left in me to deal with it. So I took the bottle and went to my office.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were exhausted. You'd given everything you had, and there was nothing left for that conversation. And the scotch — it's been your way of getting through the end of the day for a long time. That makes a certain kind of sense. And it sounds like something in that moment... still got to you. That one word.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She doesn't get it. She doesn't sit in those calls. She doesn't know what it takes to hold all of that together. My performance hasn't slipped — not once. My numbers are strong, my team respects me, I showed up to my daughter's recital last month. So I fail to see what the actual problem is here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When she said "again" — what do you think she was seeing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I don't know. Probably she's keeping some kind of tally in her head. How many nights, how much — like she's building a case. She's always been — look, she worries. That's just who she is. Her father had issues, real issues, and so she sees everything through that lens. It's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. ... You know her well enough to know where her fear comes from. And somewhere in you, you understand why she's watching.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, I do. I'm not — I'm not oblivious. I know what a bottle a night sounds like from the outside. I'm not an idiot. I just — it's different when it's you and you know your own limits and you know you're still functioning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just... hold up what I'm hearing for a second, if that's okay. You've built something remarkable — eleven years leading through crises that would break other people. You show up. You deliver. And the scotch has been part of how you do that, how you decompress, how you survive the pace you've set. And at the same time — you know how it looks. You understand your wife's fear, even if you don't agree with it. And somewhere, enough doubt crept in that you came here in the first place. All of that is true at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... That's a fair summary. I hate it, but it's fair. I don't — the reason I came here, the thing that happened, that was... that scared me. I'll admit that. But I still don't think I'm some — I'm not some out-of-control drunk.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It scared you. ... That's the first time you've said that out loud to me.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I, um... yeah. I couldn't remember driving home. Not the whole drive, I mean, I got there, clearly. But there's like a twenty-minute gap and I — I've driven that route for twelve years. And I woke up the next morning and I just sat there and thought... what if my daughter had been in the car. What if. And that thought has not left me. It hasn't left me in three weeks.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying that alone for three weeks. ... The fact that you couldn't let that thought go — that tells me something important about who you are as a father. That matters to you more than anything you've built. What do you want to do with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't — I don't want to lose everything. I didn't spend twenty years building this life to blow it up. And I think... I think maybe the way I've been managing things isn't — it's not sustainable. I don't know what that means exactly, I'm not ready to make any big declarations, but... something has to change. I can feel that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something has to change. And you're the one saying it. Not her. Not me. You.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... Yeah, I guess I am. I don't have it figured out. But I'm — I want to figure it out. I didn't come here for three months to quit now. I want to be someone my daughter isn't scared of someday. That matters more than any quarterly report.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in — I know you mentioned you're squeezed between classes, so I want to make sure we use this time well. Before anything else, I'm curious: what's your sense of why Dr. Patel thought it might be useful for the two of us to connect?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I have no idea. I went in for like, a totally standard check-up, filled out some questionnaire about drinking, and suddenly I'm being referred here like I'm some kind of... I don't know, like I have an actual problem or something. I'm a social media influencer. Going to events and drinking with people is literally what I do. It's my job.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this whole thing feels a bit out of nowhere — like the referral didn't match what you actually see as your situation.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes, I drink. But I'm at press dinners, I'm at brand launches, I'm networking, I'm creating content. My whole audience is literally built around food and wine and nightlife experiences. My friends do the same thing. It's not like I'm sitting alone in my apartment with a bottle of wine, you know? That's a completely different thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something real around this lifestyle. I'd actually love to understand it better — walk me through what a typical week looks like for you. The events, the content, all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay, so like — Monday could be a press dinner, Tuesday I might have a rooftop launch, Wednesday is usually a brand collab at some bar or restaurant, Thursday is a friend's thing, Friday and Saturday are obvious, and Sunday is brunch. It sounds like a lot when I say it out loud but that's just... the job. I'm not drinking because I'm sad or stressed or whatever. I'm drinking because I'm *there*, and being there is the whole point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being present is the whole point — and the drinking is completely woven into that world you've built. They're almost the same thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right! And I feel like everyone wants to pathologize it because it doesn't look like a regular 9-to-5. If I were sitting in some office cubicle and going to happy hour every single day after work, nobody would say anything. But because I post about it, because it's visible, suddenly I have a *problem*? That is such a double standard and it's honestly... it's kind of offensive.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like you're being held to a different standard because of your visibility. That frustration makes sense. You also mentioned some friends have brought this up — what do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, a couple of them, yeah. But Kayla sent me this whole concerned text after a night where *she* drank literally just as much as I did, so I don't really take that seriously. And my friend Jamie — Jamie is anxious about everything, like genuinely everything, so that's just her. I love her but she worries if I take the wrong exit on the freeway. I honestly think they're projecting. Or they're a little jealous that I'm not sitting at home spiraling about my choices.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And Dr. Patel — do you remember what specifically came up in that screening that made her want to refer you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She used some acronym — AUDIT something — and said my score was in the 'hazardous' range. Cool. Great label. I told her that I scored higher because I answered honestly about frequency, not because anything bad is happening, and she just kind of... looked at me. That look. And I was like, fine, I'll go talk to someone, whatever you need, here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, just to make sure I have it right. You came here because Dr. Patel referred you after a screening that raised a flag — and you genuinely disagree with that concern. The drinking is deeply tied to who you are, both professionally and socially. And when the people around you — Kayla, Jamie, Dr. Patel — bring it up, it lands as judgment rather than care. Like they're seeing something wrong in a life you've worked hard to build. Is that close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's pretty much it. I just — I don't want to sit here and be told that my whole life is wrong. Like, this is what I've worked for. This is what I've built.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's something underneath all of this that you're protecting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I guess. I built this from nothing. My mom thought I was wasting my time when I started posting. Like genuinely told me to get a real job. And now I have 400,000 followers and actual brand deals and I... I made it. So the idea that the thing that got me there — the going out, being seen, being in those rooms — might somehow be... I don't know. That's a scary thought. I don't really know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to ask you something, and take your time with it. If nothing changes — the schedule, the pace, the way things are right now — where do you see yourself in five years?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I haven't really let myself go there. I always figured I'd figure it out, you know? Like scale back when it made sense to. But when I actually try to picture it... I don't have a plan for that. I don't even know what scaling back looks like for me, or if it's even possible without losing everything I've built. That's kind of a weird thing to realize right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today under pressure, not really wanting to be here — and you stayed, and you were honest, even when some of what came up felt uncomfortable. That takes something. I'm not here to tell you your life is wrong. What I'd offer is this: you clearly care about what you've built. It might just be worth getting curious — just curious — about whether the drinking is fully serving that life, or whether it's starting to cost it something. Not a verdict. Just a question worth sitting with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Maybe. I'm not saying anything is wrong. But... maybe I can think about it. I don't know. I really do need to get to class.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I want to start by just getting a sense of where you're at — what brings you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife basically dragged me in. And my doctor's been on my case. I don't really think I need to be here, honestly. No offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because the people around you pushed for it — not necessarily because you believed something needed to change.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, look — I work construction. Hard physical work, ten, twelve hours a day out in the sun. I come home, I have a few beers. That's just... that's what guys like me do. My doctor looks at some numbers and suddenly I'm an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say 'some numbers' — what exactly did the doctor tell you about those results?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He said my liver enzymes were elevated. Threw out a bunch of numbers I didn't understand. Said I need to cut back or stop completely. I'm like — okay, I work outside all day, maybe I'm just dehydrated or something. He's making it way bigger than it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like that explanation didn't fit with how you understand your own body — you've been doing this work for years, you know yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's exactly it. Twenty years I've been doing this. I know when something's wrong with me. But then — the results came back a second time. And they were worse. And that just... that pissed me off. I don't need some doctor telling me how to run my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That second result — what did it stir up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My dad. He, uh... he died of cirrhosis. When he was 58. I was there. I watched the whole thing happen. And I swore — I swore I was never gonna let that happen to me. So when those numbers came back worse... I got in my truck and I just sat there. For like an hour. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying that — watching your father — and when that second result came back, something clicked. Like you recognized the road.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, I still think — tests can be wrong, right? But I did the detox. I did the whole ten days. So some part of me must've taken it seriously, right? That wasn't exactly a vacation.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage — walking into detox when part of you wasn't even sure you had a problem. What made you decide to go through with it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter. She's nine. She drew me this picture while I was in there — just stick figures. Me and her, fishing. She's nine years old and she's already drawing me pictures about the future. I can't be my dad. I can't do that to her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in today feeling pushed — by your wife, your doctor. But underneath that, there's a man who watched his father die from this disease, who got test results that scared him enough to sit alone in his truck for an hour, who walked himself through ten days of detox, and who has a nine-year-old daughter drawing pictures of the future she wants with her dad. That's a lot to hold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...When you say it like that. I don't know. I'm not — I'm not some drunk. I'm a good father. I show up. I work hard. I just... yeah. Maybe I do need to figure some stuff out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'figure some stuff out' — what would that actually look like for you? Not what the doctor says, not what your wife wants. What do you want?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I want to feel normal. Not need a beer to wind down at night. Not wake up feeling like garbage every morning and tell myself it's just the job. I want to be around. I want to take my kid fishing — for real, not in some drawing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've already taken the hardest first step. And what I hear is someone who knows exactly what he's fighting for — his daughter, his health, not repeating his father's story. That's not a small thing. That's everything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess it is. I'm just... I'm tired of pretending everything's fine when it's not. I think that might be the most honest thing I've said in a long time.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you reached out on your own. That's not nothing. What made today the day you decided to come in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I... my advisor pulled me aside last week. Said my last two chapters were clearly rushed. Which, honestly, they were. I knew it when I submitted them. I just kept telling myself I'd fix it later and... I don't know. I'm tired of telling myself that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about that conversation landed differently than the others.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, I've been stressed since second year, that's nothing new. But lately I've been — okay, I'll just say it — I've been drinking pretty much every night. Just to turn my brain off. And I know that's not... sustainable isn't even the right word. It's just not working anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Walk me through what that actually looks like — the drinking. What's a typical night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I get home, like 9 or 10. I tell myself I'll work a couple more hours. But I pour a drink first, just to decompress. And then the work just... doesn't happen. Three, four drinks, watch something, pass out. Wake up anxious. It's been — I don't know, four months? Maybe longer. I stopped counting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking gives you some relief in the moment, but you wake up more behind than you were — and probably more anxious on top of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And the thing is — I know this. I'm in a research program, I've literally read about the anxiety-alcohol loop. But knowing something and actually... I feel like such an idiot. Like I didn't belong here to begin with, and now I'm just proving it to everyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like carrying that thought around every day — that you don't belong?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exhausting. And I'm angry at myself because I worked so hard to get here. I was the first in my family to finish undergrad. I got a fellowship. And now I'm — I don't know. I can see myself sabotaging everything and I just... can't seem to stop doing it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The person who earned that fellowship, who was the first in his family — he's still the one sitting here. You showed up today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. But my advisor — he's not a cruel guy, he just said it flat. 'This isn't your best work.' I nodded, said I'd revise. Then I went home and drank a bottle of wine by myself and... that's when I knew. That's not coping. That's just hiding.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture finishing this PhD — the version of you that actually gets there — what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Um... I used to think about it all the time in undergrad. Calling my mom after the defense. She doesn't really understand what a PhD is, but she knows it's big. She'd cry. I... I haven't thought about that in a really long time. That's — yeah. That's actually kind of sad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've drifted a long way from that picture.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I have. And the drinking was supposed to make the gap feel smaller, you know? Like just get through tonight, deal with it tomorrow. But it just made the gap bigger. I haven't written anything real in months. I'm just... treading water. Badly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You still care about this — the research, what it means to your family, who you want to be. That hasn't gone anywhere. What would it mean to you to get that back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything. I mean — I actually like my research when I'm not drowning. Like genuinely. And I think if I got my head clear, actually slept, ate real food... I could do this. I know I could. I just need to stop running from it every night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me pull this together. You came in on your own because something your advisor said finally broke through. You've named the pattern clearly — using alcohol to manage pressure that only grows because of it. And underneath all of it, there's still a guy who wants to call his mom after his defense. That's real. So what feels like a possible first step, even a small one?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not drinking during the week. Just start there. And actually using the counseling center instead of just knowing it exists. I've been avoiding it because asking for help feels like admitting I can't handle it. But... I can't. Not right now. And I think that's okay to say.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back today. I know last week felt like a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost didn't, honestly. I sat in the parking lot for like twenty minutes. I'm not even sure why I'm here — the counselor at school keeps calling and I just... I don't know. I figured I'd come.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You almost didn't come. And yet here you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. It's not like I have a drinking problem or anything. I mean, I know that's probably what everyone thinks. My daughter keeps saying I need to talk to someone, so... I'm talking to you. I don't know what they want from me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think they're seeing that worries them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I guess I've been having a glass of wine at night. Maybe more than one. But Raymond died eight months ago and I haven't been sleeping, I haven't been eating right, and it helps me sleep. That's all it is. I raised two kids on my own when he was deployed. I'm not weak.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The wine helps you get through the nights. And you want me to understand that this isn't weakness — that you've carried hard things before and you know how to survive.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. That's right. [long pause] The nights are the worst. I'll hear something and I'll go to say, 'Raymond, did you hear that?' And then I remember. Every single time. Like my brain just keeps forgetting he's gone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like such a painful kind of loneliness. To reach for someone who isn't there anymore. [pause] I'm not going to rush past that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He was my person, you know? Forty-one years. I don't... I don't know how to be without him. I don't even know who I am anymore. [voice breaks] Sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Please don't apologize. [pause] Can I ask — who were you, with him? What did your life look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh. Um. [soft laugh] We used to garden. I had this whole vegetable garden — tomatoes, zucchini, everything. And Sunday mornings we'd walk around the neighborhood. Nothing fancy. But I... I haven't touched the garden since he died. It just felt wrong. Like I couldn't do it without him watching.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The garden waited for you. And somewhere inside, you're still the woman who grew things.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [long pause] I never thought about it like that. [quietly] I used to love it. I'd be out there in the morning with my coffee before anyone else was up. I was good at it, actually. Raymond called me his little farmer. [pause] God, I miss him so much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You came back today even when part of you wanted to stay in that parking lot. You've been getting through the nights the only way you know how right now. And there's also this woman who grew tomatoes, who took Sunday walks, who was someone's little farmer — and she's still here. She's sitting in this room with me right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [long pause] I haven't thought about the garden in months. I don't know why. Maybe I was scared. Maybe it would feel too much like moving on. And I don't want to move on. Is that terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you if moving on didn't have to mean leaving him behind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. [pause] I think... maybe I could plant something for him. In his memory. He always wanted to grow peppers and I never let him because they take up too much space. [small laugh] Maybe I could try the peppers this spring. I don't know if that's silly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's not silly at all. That's love. That's you, still in relationship with him, still carrying who he was. That impulse — to grow something for him — that's not a small thing. That's everything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quietly] Yeah, maybe it is. ... I think I want to try. I don't know about all the other stuff yet — the drinking and everything — but... maybe I start there. With the peppers.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — Marcus, right? Good. I'm glad you came in. I know this isn't exactly how most people want to spend a Wednesday afternoon. I'll be upfront with you: I'm not here to lecture you, and I'm definitely not going to tell you to stop drinking scotch. That's not my job. My job is just to... have a conversation. So — your doctor flagged some things. What's your read on all that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My read is that he overreacted. Look, I'm 45. Things shift. Enzymes fluctuate, blood pressure goes up — I've been under an enormous amount of stress this quarter. We're in the middle of an acquisition. I told him that. I don't think sitting in this office is the most productive use of my time, honestly, but... here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here you are. And you run a company — so I'm guessing you don't do things without a reason, even things that feel like a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... fair. I'm strategic about my time, yes. Look, my wife made it very clear that she wanted me to come in. The lab results gave her — I don't know — ammunition is probably the right word. She's been saying things for a while. I'm here partly to get her off my back, partly to have someone with actual credentials tell her the numbers aren't as dramatic as she's making them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the hope is I'll basically write you a permission slip. I appreciate the honesty. Tell me — when you were actually sitting in the doctor's office and he went through the results, what was that moment like for you? Not the strategic read-out afterward. That moment in the room.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... he laid out the numbers. Liver enzymes significantly elevated — his word, significantly. Blood pressure that he called stage two. And then he looked at me and asked how much I drink and I said... socially. Which is — I mean, that's not entirely inaccurate. I drink in social settings. I also drink alone. I didn't get into the specifics.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You gave him the version that felt manageable to say out loud. And you're giving me a slightly fuller version right now. That's actually... not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I suppose. I'm not — I don't lie. I just... I didn't feel like having that conversation in a twelve-minute appointment with a man I see once a year. The specifics felt beside the point. The point was the numbers. I wanted to understand the numbers.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What are the specifics? If you don't mind me asking — what does drinking actually look like for you on, say, a normal Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Tuesday. I get home — usually eight, eight-thirty. I pour a scotch. I decompress. Go through emails, maybe watch something. I'll... I'll finish the bottle, typically. By midnight, one. I've done it for fifteen years and I have not — not once — been impaired in a meeting, missed a deadline, made a bad call because of it. My performance record speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A bottle a night for fifteen years, and the lights still stay on. That's actually — I mean, I want to be real with you — that's a significant tolerance your body has built. That's not a small thing. And I hear you that the work side of things has been intact. But I'm also curious what it actually costs to maintain that. Like, not the career. The other stuff.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife would have a long answer to that question. I... we don't — she goes to bed at ten. We don't have a lot of evenings together anymore. She says I'm not really present even when I'm home. Which I think is... I mean, I work the hours I work. That's a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Is it a separate issue?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I don't know. Maybe not entirely. She's — she's not wrong that I'm different in the evenings. I'm aware of that. It's just that the version of me at eight PM who's had three drinks is the only version of me that can actually sit still. Sober me at eight PM is still running the morning's meeting in my head. I don't know how to — I've never really known how to turn that off any other way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the scotch isn't the problem — it's the solution. The only solution you've found that actually works. Except now the solution is starting to show up on a lab report. And in your wife's face.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's a pretty accurate framing. I don't love it, but. And the thing is — I know. I'm not an idiot. I know what a bottle a night means medically. I've known for a while. I just — I've been able to not think about it because everything else was working.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And now something's making it harder to not think about it. If you zoom out — ten, fifteen years from now — what does this look like if nothing changes? Not worst-case disaster scenario. Just... honest projection, the way you'd run the numbers on a business decision.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? The numbers don't work. I know that. Liver disease, cardiovascular — I've read enough. And my wife... she's patient, but she's not infinitely patient. I think I've been betting that I could manage it indefinitely and the lab results were basically the market telling me my model is flawed. I don't ignore market signals. I've just been ignoring this one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to just — take a second and reflect back what I've heard, because I think you've said more in the last twenty minutes than you maybe expected to. You came in skeptical, ready to walk out with a clean bill of health. But you've also told me: you know the numbers, you've known for a while, the drinking is solving something real for you — the off-switch problem — and that the cost is showing up in your health, and in the distance between you and your wife. That's a lot of honest. And for someone who's never talked to anyone about this before — that's not nothing. So. What do you want to do with any of this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know exactly. Which is a weird thing for me to say. I usually know. But I think — I think I want to figure out if there's another off-switch. Because this one's got a leak in it and I can't keep pretending it doesn't. So. Yeah. I'll come back.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi, I'm really glad you made it in today. I know it's not always easy walking through a new door — especially when it wasn't entirely your idea. There's nowhere we need to get to today. We can just... talk.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean — thanks. I just want to be upfront about something, because I feel like I should just say it: I don't actually think there's a problem here. My friends kind of staged this whole thing and it got really emotional and I love them so much, so I'm here. But I feel like I'm being treated like some kind of cautionary tale, which is honestly a little... I don't know. Insulting isn't quite the right word. Just... off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up for them. Even not being sure this is where you belong — you came anyway. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mia was crying. I can't — I physically cannot watch Mia cry and just do nothing, you know? But I think they all misunderstand what my life actually looks like. Like, I'm a content creator. Going out, being seen, building energy in a room — that's literally my job. It's not like I'm drinking alone in the dark. It's my career.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like, being in that room with them? When Mia was crying?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Awful. Like — awful. It felt like being put on trial. Everyone going around saying their piece in a circle and I'm just sitting there thinking, is this really how you all see me? Because I don't see myself that way. At all. And there's something really disorienting about the people who are supposed to know you best looking at you like... like you're a problem to be solved.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You sat in that room, heard some really hard things from people who clearly love you, and you didn't leave. You stayed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: *small laugh* I thought about it. Not gonna lie. But... yeah. I stayed. I don't know, I just keep going back and forth — part of me is like, everyone's overreacting, this is so dramatic. And then there's this other part that has, like... a flash of something. And then I immediately push it away and I'm back on Instagram and it's gone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a flash of something... and then you push it away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't even — I'm not sure what it is exactly. Sometimes after a really big night I wake up and there's this... heaviness. Not a hangover, I'm way past hangovers. Just like, a grey feeling. And I let myself sit with it for maybe thirty seconds and then I'm up, I'm making coffee, I'm posting my morning routine. It's fine. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine your life — your actual life, not the feed — what matters most to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Connection. Genuinely. I love people. I love being in a room full of energy and laughter and — I've built this whole world around that. And I love it, I really do. But sometimes I wonder if... *trails off* no, I don't know where I was going with that. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Connection is at the center of everything for you. And somewhere in the middle of that thought, something else showed up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I was going to say, I sometimes wonder if those people would still be around if there wasn't a bar involved. Like — is it me they love, or is it the version of me that shows up after drink two? The fun one, the one who knows everyone, who makes the whole room feel electric. I've never actually let myself think about that for very long.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — you came here for Mia, because you love her, and you stayed even when every part of you wanted to walk out. You've described this grey feeling that visits some mornings and then disappears. There's a real question underneath everything about who you are when the room empties out. And at the same time, you've built something genuinely meaningful — a community, a career, a life that runs on connection. That's a lot to be holding all at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it all back to me like that it sounds... *pause* ...it doesn't sound great, does it. But I still — I want to be clear, I still don't think I have a problem. I think I have a very full life and a very anxious friend group and maybe I just need to post less so people worry less. That's probably it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just sat with some really uncomfortable things. And you didn't brush past them — even though you are clearly very, very good at doing exactly that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: *laughs softly* I have a whole aesthetic built around making everything look effortless and golden. So. Yeah, I am very good at that. But... okay. I don't know. Maybe it's not the worst thing to just sit with something for a second. Just a second. I'm not promising anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you to let yourself keep looking at this — even just a little?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I have no idea. Maybe I look and find out I'm totally fine and everyone can relax and I can go back to my life. Or maybe... I don't know. I genuinely don't know. But I'm back here Thursday apparently, so. I guess we'll see.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you reached out. That takes something, you know — picking up the phone, setting this up. So... what's been weighing on you lately? What made this feel like the right time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My coworker — Janet — she pulled me aside last week and said she was... concerned. About me. And I don't know, it kind of blindsided me. I mean, I'm doing my job. My kids are fine, my classes are fine. I just — I don't really think I needed someone at work getting into my personal life, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It felt like an intrusion. Someone stepping into something that you hadn't invited them into.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like, I've been teaching for eleven years. Eleven. I haven't had a single complaint, my evaluations are good, I coach the chess club — which nobody else wanted to do, by the way. And now suddenly I'm someone who needs to be... checked on? It's — I don't know. It just felt off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eleven years. That's a lot of yourself poured into that building. I'm curious — when you get home at the end of the day, what does that look like for you? Like, how do you decompress?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. I mean, I get home around four-thirty, four-forty-five. I change out of my work clothes. Usually I'll have a drink — maybe two — while I make dinner. Watch something. I dunno, it's just... it's how I wind down. It's not like I'm drinking in the parking lot or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes sense — teaching middle schoolers is genuinely exhausting work. The emotional labor alone... you're holding a lot every single day. And you've built a structure that helps you transition out of that headspace.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Yeah. I mean, it is a lot. People don't — they don't get what it's like to be in a room with thirty thirteen-year-olds for six hours. Every day. You can't just... flip a switch when you get home. You need something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You need something. I hear that. I want to ask you something gently, and I hope it's okay — there were some mornings, you said occasionally... where things were harder? Where you maybe didn't feel quite right going in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — look, everyone has rough mornings. That's not — that's not specific to me. And the times where I felt off, I still went in. I still did my job. I didn't call out. So I don't know what we're supposed to make of that. I'm not like... I'm not some guy who can't function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up. Even on the hard days, you showed up. And... there's also this part of you that reached out today. Those two things are both true at the same time — the guy who holds it together, and the guy who thought maybe something needed a closer look.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I don't know. I guess. I mean, yeah, I made the call. But I'm still not — I'm not sitting here thinking I have some big problem. It's more like... I don't know, Janet's comment stuck with me more than I wanted it to. That's all. It bothered me that it bothered me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just... hold a few things together for a second, if that's okay. You've got eleven years of showing up, you're clearly someone who cares deeply about your work and your students. You've got this routine that helps you get through what is genuinely hard work. And then there's Janet's comment — which you didn't shrug off, even though part of you wanted to. And something in you picked up the phone. I don't think that's nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
No. Yeah. It's... it's not nothing.

I think — if I'm being honest, and I don't really say this out loud — I think some mornings I feel kind of... ashamed. Going in. And I hate that. I hate that feeling.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That shame you just named — that took courage to say. What do you think that feeling is telling you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
I think it's telling me that I... I know, on some level, that it's gotten to be more than it should be. Like, I'm not oblivious. I went from maybe a drink or two to — sometimes it's more. And I keep telling myself it's fine because I'm still functional, still showing up. But there's this voice that's like... is this who you are? Is this who you want to be?

And I don't know. I don't have an answer for that yet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You heard that voice and you didn't run from it. You sat with it long enough to be here, talking about it. That matters — it really does. The fact that you can name what's happening, that you care about the kind of person you are... that's not something everyone has access to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I want to be someone my students would respect, right? Like, if they knew — if they could see me at ten PM sometimes, just... I don't want that. I got into teaching because I actually care about these kids. I don't want to be someone who's just going through the motions.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That person — the one who cares, who shows up for those kids, who coaches chess club when no one else will — he's still in there. And it sounds like part of why you're here is to make sure he gets to stick around.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think so. I mean, I'm not ready to like... make any big declarations or whatever. But yeah. I think that's — yeah. That's why I called.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for making time for this today. So you reached out on your own, which — I just want to say — takes some guts. What's been going on for you lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't even know where to start. I've been painting for like fifteen years, right, and I always — alcohol was just part of it, you know? Like, it loosens something up. But lately my work has been... I don't know. Flat. And my dealer — my gallery dealer, not like a drug dealer — she said something at my last show that I can't stop thinking about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ha — appreciate the clarification on the dealer. What did she say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said the new pieces feel... muddy. Like emotionally muddy. And I got so angry at first — who is she, you know? But then I went home and looked at them and... god, she's right. They're muddy. I used to make things that made people cry. Now I'm making beige.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you went home, you looked at your own work with fresh eyes, and you saw what she saw. That must have hit hard — especially coming from someone whose opinion actually matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. I cried, actually. Which... I haven't cried in a while. And I started thinking — like, I always told myself the wine was helping. That's the whole myth, right? Tortured artist, a little drunk, makes great work. That's the story I've been living inside.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The tortured artist myth. It's a powerful one — honestly, it's practically got a PR team at this point. What's it been like, living inside that story?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Comfortable, I guess? Like it gave me permission. Every glass was practically a creative decision. I was... I was romanticizing it. But if the work is getting worse, then what's the point? What am I even doing?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to sit with — you built an identity around something, and now the evidence from your own work is starting to poke holes in it. And instead of defending the story, you're actually questioning it. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess. I don't know if I'm questioning it so much as panicking about it. Like, what if I can't make anything without it? What if the wine isn't dulling me — what if it's the only thing keeping me from being completely blocked? That's the thing that scares me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there are two fears kind of living side by side here — one is that the alcohol is already hurting the work, and the other is that without it, there might be... nothing there. Like it's a floor and a ceiling at the same time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly that. God, that's... yeah. Both things are true and they completely contradict each other and I've been sitting with that for weeks and it's exhausting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I share something? A lot of artists — writers, musicians, painters — have talked about this exact fear. And what research and a lot of recovery narratives show is that the creativity doesn't come from the substance. It was always yours. The alcohol just lowered the inhibition enough that you could access it... but it's a loan, and the interest rate gets brutal over time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The interest rate. Yeah. I feel like I've been paying that. The hangovers are longer now, I'm slower in the mornings, I'm... I picked up a brush last Tuesday at like 10am and I just sat there. Completely empty. And I had a glass of wine to get going and then another and by afternoon I had made one mark on the canvas. One.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One mark. After a whole day. And you came here anyway. What do you think that says about you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I'm... stubborn? Or maybe just scared enough to finally do something. I don't want to lose this. Painting is the only thing I've ever been sure about. If I lose that because I was too precious about my little ritual... I don't know. I think I'd hate myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing across this whole conversation, because I think you've said some really important things. You came here because something cracked open — your dealer's words, your own eyes looking at your work. You've been living inside a story that gave you permission to drink, but you're starting to see the cost of that story. You're scared that without alcohol there's nothing there — but honestly? The fact that you made work that made people cry for fifteen years? That came from you, not from a bottle. And you love painting too much to keep gambling with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... it sounds less like I have a drinking problem and more like I've been afraid of myself. Of what I actually am without the... costume. Is that weird?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not weird at all — that might actually be the most insightful thing said in a first session I've heard in a long time. So what would it mean for you to start getting to know that person? The one without the costume?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think it would mean actually finding out if I'm good. Like really finding out. Which is terrifying. But also — I kind of want to know. I haven't wanted anything in a while. That feels like something.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you today. Last time we talked, things felt like they were moving... and then you mentioned things got harder this week. I just want to sit with that for a moment. What's been going on for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't even know where to start. It's just... last week felt okay, like I actually had a couple nights where I only had one glass, and I thought, okay, maybe I'm doing this. And then my ex called about switching weekends and it just... unraveled. I ended up finishing the whole bottle both nights after that. So. I don't know. Back to square one I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You had two really good nights. That wasn't nothing — you did that. And then one phone call pulled the rug out from under you, and it hurt.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. It did. He's just so — he doesn't think about how it affects the kids, you know? Or me. And I'm standing there in the kitchen after getting off the phone and I'm just... I'm so tired. Like, bone-tired. And the wine was right there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That exhaustion you're describing — it sounds like it goes way deeper than just a bad week. Like you've been carrying something really heavy for a long time, and sometimes the only thing that makes the weight feel bearable, even for a few hours, is that bottle.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. That's... that's exactly it. I keep telling myself it's fine, it's just wine, it's just how I unwind. But if I'm honest? I don't think I know how to get through the evenings without it anymore. And that scares me. It really scares me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took courage to say. It really did. What is it that scares you most when you sit with that thought?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That my kids are going to figure it out. Emma's twelve. She's not stupid. I see her sometimes looking at me when I pour the second glass, and... I just. I don't want to be that mom. My mom was... she had her own stuff. And I swore I wouldn't do that to them. And here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that Emma's face comes to mind in that moment... that tells me something about who you are as a mother. You're watching yourself. You care so deeply about not repeating what was done to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But caring isn't enough, is it? I mean, my mom probably cared too. I don't know. Maybe she didn't. But I just... I feel like I'm failing them every single night and I can't stop. Like, what is wrong with me? Why can't I just... not?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nothing is wrong with you. You are a person in a tremendous amount of pain, with almost no support, doing this almost completely alone. The wine is doing something for you — it's been your way of surviving. The problem isn't that you're broken. The problem is that the only tool you have right now isn't working anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I never thought about it like that.

I just always figured I was weak. Like, other people manage. Other single moms manage.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Other single moms aren't you, with your history, your load, your ex, your two kids, doing it without a safety net. You've been comparing your insides to everyone else's outsides for a long time, haven't you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Yeah. Yeah, I have. My friend Sarah, she makes it look so easy, and I'm over here just... white-knuckling everything. But she has a husband. She has family nearby. I don't have any of that. I hadn't really let myself think about how different our situations actually are.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So when you set those two good nights aside — the ones your ex disrupted — and you think about what made them possible... what was different on those nights?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? The kids were both in a good mood. There was no drama at dinner. I had called my sister that afternoon, just to talk. And I made myself go for a walk before they got home. Just like, twenty minutes. But I felt... I don't know. Like I had a little bit of me left by the time I got to bedtime.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just described something really important. When you had even a sliver of connection — your sister, your own body, a bit of quiet — you didn't need the wine the same way. That's not small. That's actually the whole map.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't even realize I was doing it. I just thought those were good days because of the kids. But maybe... maybe I helped make them good days? I don't know, that sounds kind of... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think you might not be fully seeing what you've just said. You came in today feeling like you were back at square one. But you told me about two nights you chose differently. You named the exact conditions that helped. You're connecting your own patterns, in real time, right now. That's not someone who's failing. That's someone who's figuring it out — slowly, painfully, but figuring it out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I really needed to hear that today.

I don't know if I believed it before, but... I think I actually believe it right now.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So before we dive into anything heavy — full disclosure, I saw in your file this isn't your first rodeo with counseling. I'm not going to run you through the same script you've already heard. That seems like a waste of both our time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My therapist basically guilted me into coming here. Said you were more 'specialized,' whatever that means. I'm fine. I just — I drink, like, every artist drinks. That's not some big revelation that needs a whole clinic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Got it — so you're here more for her than for you right now. I'm curious though, what's the thing she's most worried about that you think she's getting completely wrong?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She hears 'drinks every day' and goes straight to — I mean, she literally pulled out a pamphlet. A pamphlet. What am I, eighteen? I use alcohol to get into a headspace for my work. That's not a problem, that's a process. Plenty of great artists have done exactly that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's less about being out of control and more that — you've built a system. Alcohol is part of the architecture of how you create.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And nobody in these kinds of offices ever actually gets that. You're all trained to see a diagnosis, not a person. My last counselor — I threw his pamphlet in the parking lot on the way out. True story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The parking lot. Efficient. Okay — so help me understand the system. What does a good creative day actually look like for you? Walk me through it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It used to be — I'd start around noon, have a glass or two, get past the... the noise. The critic in my head. And by mid-afternoon I'd just be in it. The work would come. Now I do the same exact thing and I'm just... sitting there staring. I've got six canvases I haven't touched in months.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know exactly what that zone feels like — you've lived there. And you're measuring everything against it. That level of self-awareness about your own creative process, that's actually not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well it's not helping me much when I'm staring at a blank canvas at two in the afternoon with a glass of Pinot Grigio thinking 'this should be working.' I'm making garbage. I look at stuff I painted three years ago and I barely recognize myself in it. It's like someone else made those.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's real grief in that. Looking at your own older work and feeling like a stranger to it — that's not a small thing to carry around.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's been... close to a year now. I keep telling myself it's a block, that I'll break through if I just push harder. But the pushing harder isn't... it's not doing anything. I'm doing all the same things and it's just getting worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I share something that might be a little uncomfortable to hear? There's this thing that can happen — the brain adapts to whatever we give it repeatedly. What used to quiet the inner critic, over time, can start feeding it instead. I'm not saying that's what's happening. I just... I wonder if part of you is already asking that question.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... maybe. I've thought about it. Like — am I using it to create, or am I just using it to feel less anxious about creating? Because those aren't the same thing. I know that. I just... I don't really like sitting with that question very long.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you if the thing you thought was unlocking the door has actually been, slowly, changing the lock?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... I've been wrong about myself for a really long time. And I've built — I have this whole identity around being someone who creates. If that's broken, or if I'm the one who broke it, then... I don't know what I am outside of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's not really about the alcohol at all, is it. It's about who you are if the story you've been telling yourself about creativity turns out to be more complicated than you thought.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And that's... that's the part that's actually terrifying. I don't even know what I'd do differently. But I also can't keep making things I hate. That was never supposed to be what this was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold what you've brought in today. You came in not particularly wanting to be here, with a real and honestly pretty defensible belief that alcohol is part of your creative process — that's not a crazy story, a lot of artists have told it. But you also know the work has shifted. Nearly a year of making things you don't recognize, don't love. And underneath all of that is this question you've been circling: what if the thing that was supposed to open you up has been quietly closing you down? You haven't answered it. But you didn't walk out either.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm still sitting here. That's... something, I guess. I don't have an answer. But I'm not — I'm not ready to throw that question in the parking lot. Not this time.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Marcus — everyone just calls me Marcus, the whole 'doctor' thing gets old fast. Can I grab you some water before we get going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. I'm fine. ... Um, how long is this actually supposed to take? I have class second period.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair question — nobody's ever excited to be in one of these chairs, especially the first time. So let me just ask: what's your understanding of why you're here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because someone ratted me out at homecoming and now literally everyone's acting like I robbed a bank. I had two drinks. Two. And everyone there was doing the exact same thing — I'm just the one who got caught. It's so unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the whole thing felt like you got singled out — like you were doing what everyone does and somehow ended up being the example.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Thank you. My mom, my school counselor, now my doctor sending me here — they're all acting like I have some kind of problem. I'm eighteen. I had two beers at a party. That's not... that's not like, an alcoholic. That's just being a teenager.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you being upfront about that. And for what it's worth — I'm not here to pin a label on you or tell you you have a problem. That's genuinely not my thing. I'm just curious: what's it actually like at those parties, for you personally?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... fun? It's just what you do to loosen up. You can't just stand there being awkward and sober while everyone else is having a good time. That's like, social suicide.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Social survival is a real thing — I don't want to wave that off. Navigating all that at eighteen is genuinely hard. What do you think would happen if you didn't drink at one of those parties?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd be the awkward one in the corner on my phone while everyone else is laughing and having fun. My friends would notice. They'd probably think something was wrong with me, or like... that I was judging them or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's a real cost in your mind — being seen as different, maybe losing that sense of fitting in. That's actually a really honest thing to say, and most people take way longer to get there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean. I never really said it out loud like that. It's not like I even love drinking. It's more like... it just makes things easier, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Easier than what?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Easier than just being... me, I guess. Like, sober me at a party is just kind of in her head the whole time. Worried about what she looks like, what she's saying, if people think she's weird. But after like one or two drinks that whole... loop just stops. For a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if I'm hearing you right — this was never really about the alcohol. The alcohol is solving something for you. The anxiety, the self-consciousness, the loop you're describing. The drink is the off switch. That's a pretty different thing than 'just doing what everyone else does.'

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, I — huh. No one's ever said it like that before. I always just thought I was like, socially awkward and that was just how it was. I didn't really connect the two things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like to hear yourself say that out loud?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Kind of... weird? But also like — okay this is going to sound dumb — but kind of relieved? Like maybe there's actually something there that could be figured out. It's not just me being a bad kid. There's like a reason.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound dumb at all. That sounds like someone starting to understand herself — and that's genuinely hard work. You came in here ready to fight me, and instead you just did something most adults struggle to do. I think there's a lot more worth exploring, but that right there? That's a real start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Okay. I mean, I'm not like, promising anything. But I guess I can come back. Maybe.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time today. Doing this over video — sometimes that actually makes it a little easier to talk. So, what made you decide to reach out now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My doctor scared me into it. Said my liver numbers were... not great. I figured I should talk to somebody, but I'm not sure any of this is gonna do much good, you know? I'm not some kind of — I don't know. I just figured I'd come.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is skeptical this will help, and at the same time — those numbers were bad enough that you picked up the phone anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. He actually sat me down. Didn't just hand me a printout and wave me off. That's... that's never happened before. So I figured, alright.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what life's been like since you retired. What changed for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything changed. I worked 38 years, okay? Forty hours minimum, usually more. And then one day it just... stops. And you're supposed to what, golf? My wife passed four years ago, my kids have their own lives, and I'm just — I don't know, it's a lot of nothing. A lot of quiet. And I didn't sign up for quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thirty-eight years of having somewhere to be, somewhere you mattered — and then silence.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's it exactly. I didn't realize how much of who I was was tied up in that job until it was gone. Kind of embarrassing to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When did the drinking start fitting into that picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I always had a drink or two at night. But after I retired it became... more. Because what else am I doing? It's five o'clock and I'm sitting in this house alone and it just takes the edge off. The quiet gets loud, if that makes sense. And I'm not hurting anybody.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking gives you some relief from that noise in the quiet. And you said something else — that you're not hurting anybody. Sounds like that's a thought you come back to a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess it is. Because when he showed me those numbers I thought, I'm not some drunk stumbling around, I'm a guy having a few drinks in his own house. But then I thought — I mean, my liver doesn't care about my excuses, does it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your liver doesn't care about your excuses. What does that land on for you when you say it out loud like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to be sick. I have two grandkids — seven and ten. And I think about them. I want to be around. I want to take them fishing like my grandfather took me. I haven't done that yet. I keep putting it off and I... I don't even know why I keep putting it off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You carry that image — taking your grandkids out on the water the way your grandfather did for you. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
