utterances.text: It's not small, no. And sitting in that recliner every night drinking by myself... that's not who I want to be for them. Or for me, honestly. I just — I didn't want to say that because then I'd have to actually do something about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't want to admit it because admitting it meant acting on it. That's a real thing. So — what would acting on it look like? What feels like a first step you could actually see yourself taking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I need to call my doctor first. I've heard you can't just quit cold turkey — that can be dangerous. So do it right. And there's this senior center I drive past every week. Every single week. Maybe it's time I actually pull into the parking lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing. You came in skeptical, but something real brought you here — your doctor, your liver, your grandkids, a version of yourself you want to get back to. You've been honest about what the drinking fills — that emptiness retirement left behind — and you haven't pretended that's easy to sit with. And now you're talking about calling your doctor, cutting back safely, and finally walking into that senior center. You came in saying you weren't sure this would do any good. Look where you are now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I still don't know if I can pull it off. But I want to try. That's more than I could've said this morning.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for joining. I know doing this over video isn't always ideal, but I appreciate you being here. So — I'm not gonna pretend I don't know the context. Court sent you. But I'm curious what this is actually like for you, showing up today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What it's like? I'll tell you what it's like. It's complete bullshit, that's what it's like. I'm sitting in my own house being forced to talk to a stranger because some judge who doesn't know me decided I need — what, therapy? I had two beers. Two. And I got nailed because I was unlucky, not because I'm some kind of drunk.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two beers, and suddenly your whole life is getting restructured by people who don't know you from Adam. That's a lot of control taken away from you at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I've been working the same job for twelve years, I raise my kid half the time, I pay my taxes — and now I'm... I'm a criminal? Because of a Tuesday night? My buddy Dave drinks way more than me and nobody's hauling him into court. The whole system is just — it's targeting people, man. It's not about safety, it's about money.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built a real life — steady job, showing up for your kid. That matters, and I hear you that this feels wildly out of proportion to what you think happened. Can I ask — and you don't have to answer any way but honestly — this is the second DUI. What was going on the first time around?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... That was different. That was like five years ago, I was going through my divorce, it was a bad time. And I handled it. I did the classes, I paid the fines, done. I don't see why they get to keep using that against me forever. Like, when does it stop being on your record, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the first time was wrapped up in the divorce, a really hard stretch. And this one — what was going on in your life around the time of this second one?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... work's been a nightmare. My supervisor is — look, it doesn't matter. And the custody thing got complicated again. My ex filed some motion, so there's lawyers involved again, which means money, which means stress, and I just... I went out. That's it. I went out with some guys from work and I had a few drinks and I drove home the same way I've driven home a hundred times.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sounds like everything kind of stacked up — work, the custody fight, money — and drinking was the release valve. And you've used that same valve before, sounds like, when things got bad with the divorce.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I never thought about it like that. I mean — yeah, I guess when things pile up I, um... okay but that's just how people cope. That's normal. That's not a disorder or whatever you're gonna say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not here to hand you a diagnosis. I'm genuinely just trying to understand how things work for you. I do want to mention something though — and tell me if this is off base — I saw in your file there were some lab results flagged recently. How are you feeling about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The labs. Yeah. My doctor said my liver enzymes are... elevated, or something. He wanted to talk about my drinking and I basically said I'd think about it and got out of there. I don't know. I'm 38, not 60. That stuff happens, right? People have elevated whatever and it doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You got out of there fast.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well... I didn't want to hear it. I mean, if something's actually wrong — I have a kid. She's nine. And the custody stuff is already... if I get sick on top of all this, I don't know what happens. I don't even want to think about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That landed somewhere real just now. Your daughter. That's what you're actually scared about — not the labs, not the court. Her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. She's the — yeah. I don't want her to see me as the guy who screwed everything up. She already has to deal with the divorce stuff, switching houses, all of it. And now this. I just keep thinking, like... what does she think when she hears court, DUI, all that? She's nine, she understands more than people think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The dad you want to be for her — that guy sounds really different from the picture the last couple years have been painting. You've got the court, the labs, the stress, the drinking when things pile up. I'm not saying you're a bad person, not even close. But I'm curious what you think it would take to close that gap — between who you are right now and the dad you're describing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean... honestly? I don't know if I'd even know where to start. I'm not — I don't think I'm an alcoholic or whatever. But I'm also not gonna sit here and say the last couple years have been great, because they haven't. Maybe I do lean on it more than I should. I've never really said that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I've heard today, because I think you said some important things. You came in furious — and honestly, that made complete sense given the situation. But underneath that, there's a guy who's been carrying a lot: a stressful job, a custody battle, some scary news from your doctor, and a pattern of reaching for alcohol when the pressure gets too high — something you recognize now, even if you've never named it. And at the center of all of it is your daughter, and who you want to be for her. That's not nothing. That's actually a lot to work with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean — yeah, that's pretty much it. I didn't think I'd actually talk today. I figured I'd just sit here and clock my hours. But, um... okay. I guess I can come back next week.
